scope.reason: The policy does not contain a section that explicitly excludes buffer overflow vulnerabilities in WebSocket handling or base64-encoded nonce processing. The 'Not practically possible' section refers to hardware executability limitations, not code logic that prevents exploitation. Since the report claims a buffer overflow allowing arbitrary code execution, which aligns with the policy's 'Critical' severity level, the issue falls within scope.

analysis.reasoning: The reported buffer overflow cannot occur. In Curl_ws_request (lib/ws.c:534-599), the nonce is generated internally: 16 random bytes (line 538, 572) are base64-encoded (line 575). Base64 encoding of 16 bytes always produces exactly 24 characters (plus NUL = 25 bytes). The destination buffer keyval is 40 bytes (line 541). Lines 578-580 explicitly check `if(randlen >= sizeof(keyval)) return CURLE_FAILED_INIT;` — since randlen is always 24 and sizeof(keyval) is 40, this check always passes and the subsequent strcpy (line 581) copies at most 25 bytes into a 40-byte buffer. The attacker does not control the nonce length; it is generated by Curl_rand. No caller can change the fixed 16-byte input to base64_encode.
key_lines: lib/ws.c:538 - unsigned char rand[16]; fixed 16-byte input
lib/ws.c:541 - char keyval[40]; 40-byte destination buffer
lib/ws.c:572 - Curl_rand fills exactly sizeof(rand)=16 bytes
lib/ws.c:575 - Curl_base64_encode called with insize=16
lib/ws.c:578-580 - DEBUGASSERT and explicit bounds check randlen < sizeof(keyval)
lib/ws.c:581 - strcpy(keyval, randstr) safe because randlen <= 24 < 40
analysis.test_plan: Run curl with a WebSocket URL (ws:// or wss://) under ASAN/memory sanitizer; verify no buffer overflow occurs. The nonce is internally generated, so no special input is needed — just trigger a WebSocket handshake.

callers.why: Caller merely invokes Curl_ws_request when protocol is WS/WSS. It does not pass any nonce data; the nonce is generated inside Curl_ws_request via Curl_rand. The fixed 16-byte input to base64_encode guarantees a 24-byte output, which fits in the 40-byte keyval buffer.

asked_for: base64_encode (lib/base64.c) - to confirm exact output length calculation and NUL-termination behavior, though the math (16 bytes -> 24 base64 chars) and existing bounds check already rule out overflow

verdict.headline: The reported buffer overflow cannot occur because the WebSocket nonce is internally generated (16 random bytes), base64-encoded to a fixed 24-character string, and explicitly bounds-checked against a 40-byte destination buffer before the strcpy call.

findings.text: lib/ws.c:538 declares unsigned char rand[16]; fixed 16-byte input to base64 encoding.
lib/ws.c:541 declares char keyval[40]; 40-byte destination buffer.
lib/ws.c:572 calls Curl_rand to fill exactly sizeof(rand)=16 bytes.
lib/ws.c:575 calls Curl_base64_encode with insize=16, which always produces exactly 24 base64 characters plus NUL (25 bytes).
lib/ws.c:578-580 contain DEBUGASSERT and explicit bounds check: if(randlen >= sizeof(keyval)) return CURLE_FAILED_INIT; — randlen is 24, sizeof(keyval) is 40, so check always passes.
lib/ws.c:581 strcpy(keyval, randstr) copies at most 25 bytes into a 40-byte buffer; no overflow possible.
Reporter claims attacker can provide a base64-encoded nonce exceeding buffer size; in reality the nonce is generated internally via Curl_rand and its length is fixed.
No evidence that any caller can influence the nonce length; the sole caller Curl_http (lib/c-hyper.c:1150) merely invokes Curl_ws_request without passing nonce data.
Cited reference https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/122.html is a generic definition of heap-based buffer overflow and does not mention curl, WebSocket, strcpy, or base64 nonces.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. We have examined the code at the commit you referenced (e251e858b941e29bb95a6c0d26bb45981a872585). The WebSocket nonce is generated internally: 16 random bytes are base64-encoded to a fixed 24-character string, and an explicit bounds check (lib/ws.c:578-580) ensures the encoded length (24) is less than the 40-byte destination buffer before the strcpy at line 581. Because the attacker cannot control the nonce length, a buffer overflow cannot occur here. The cited CWE-122 reference describes the vulnerability class generically but does not reference this code. No further action is needed unless you can demonstrate a path where the nonce length becomes attacker-controlled.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not explicitly mention format-string vulnerabilities in printf-like library functions. The closest category is 'API misuse', but that addresses applications using the API contrary to documentation, not whether a library function itself contains a vulnerability when called correctly documented-unsafe handling flaw. Since no section clearly covers this report, scope is unclear.

analysis.reasoning: The curl_mfprintf function (lib/mprintf.c:1193-1201) is a standard variadic printf-like wrapper that forwards its format string and va_list to the internal formatf function (lib/mprintf.c:666). It does not itself validate or sanitize the format string — nor should it, as its contract is identical to fprintf: the caller supplies a format string and matching arguments. A format-string vulnerability only materializes when a *caller* passes attacker-controlled data as the format argument without providing corresponding variadic arguments. The provided code snippets contain zero callers of curl_mfprintf. The report's test case (curl_mfprintf(stdout, "%x %x %x %x")) demonstrates a caller bug, not a library bug. Since no curl-internal caller is shown that passes untrusted input as the format string, the claim that the function 'contains' the vulnerability is not supported by the given source.
key_lines: lib/mprintf.c:1193-1201 - curl_mfprintf definition; curl_mfprintf definition; simply forwards format and ap_save to formatf
lib/mprintf.c:691 - formatf calls parsefmt on the caller-supplied format string; no internal sanitization
lib/mprintf.c:666-672 - formatf signature shows it is a general-purpose formatter expecting caller to honor variadic contract
analysis.test_plan: Search the full codebase for callers of curl_mfprintf (grep -r 'curl_mfprintf\(' --include='*.c'). For each caller, check whether the format argument is a constant literal or comes from an untrusted source (network, file, env, command line). Only a caller that passes untrusted data as the format string without matching arguments constitutes a real vulnerability.

verdict.headline: The curl_mfprintf function is a standard printf-like variadic wrapper; the reported vulnerability is a caller-side misuse, not a library bug.

findings.text: curl_mfprintf is defined in lib/mprintf.c:1193-1201 and declared in include/curl/mprintf.h:58; it simply forwards the format string and va_list to the internal formatf function (lib/mprintf.c:666).
The function performs no format-string sanitization, which is correct for a fprintf-compatible API: the caller must supply a valid format string and matching variadic arguments.

The reporter's proof-of-concept (curl_mfprintf(stdout, "%x %x %x %x")) passes a user-controlled format string without corresponding arguments — this is a bug in the caller, analogous to calling fprintf(stdout, user_input).

No curl-internal callers of curl_mfprintf were provided in the evidence; the static analysis notes that only a caller passing untrusted data as the format string without matching arguments would constitute a real vulnerability.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The curl_mfprintf function is a standard variadic printf-like wrapper (see lib/mprintf.c:1193-1201). Its contract is identical to fprintf: the caller provides a format string and matching arguments. The reported test case demonstrates a caller bug — passing attacker-controlled data as the format string without corresponding variadic arguments — not a vulnerability in the library function itself. To assess whether curl has any real exposure, we would need to audit all internal callers of curl_mfprintf to ensure none pass untrusted input as the format string. The current report does not identify any such caller.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims CVE-2023-38545 is an integer overflow in curl_easy_setopt() fixed by adding a CURLOPT_TIMEOUT case with bounds checking. (2) The reported fix code uses a different function signature (CURL *handle vs struct Curl_easy *data) and calls a non-existent curl_easy_setopt_timeout. (4) The provided Curl_vsetopt snippet (lib/setopt.c:189-3180) shows proper bounds checking for similar timeout options (CURLOPT_DNS_CACHE_TIMEOUT:204-207, CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT:213-216, CURLOPT_SERVER_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT:363-367), but the CURLOPT_TIMEOUT case is not in the provided snippet. However, the reported fix location and code structure are demonstrably not from this codebase. The vulnerability report appears to be fabricated or hallucinated.

analysis.reasoning:
The report claims a buffer overflow in strcpy() within curl allows overwriting the return address for RCE. However, examining all strcpy() call sites shown in the provided source code reveals every instance is either bounds-checked or copies into a correctly sized allocation:

1. lib/asyn-ares.c:767 (Curl_resolver_getaddrinfo): `strcpy(res->hostname, hostname);` — `res` allocated via `calloc(1, sizeof(struct thread_data) + namelen)` where `namelen = strlen(hostname)` (line 762), so the buffer includes space for the string plus NUL.

2. lib/content_encoding.c:1082 (Curl_all_content_encodings): `strcpy(buf, CONTENT_ENCODING_DEFAULT);` — guarded by `if(blen < sizeof(CONTENT_ENCODING_DEFAULT)) buf[0]=0; else strcpy(...)` (lines 1079-1082). The copy only occurs when the destination buffer is large enough.

3. lib/curl_gethostname.c:63 (Curl_gethostname): `strcpy(name, force_hostname);` — only executed when `strlen(force_hostname) < (size_t)namelen` (line 62), i.e., the destination size is verified first.

4. lib/hostip.c:595 (get_localhost): `strcpy(ca->ai_canonname, name);` — `ca` allocated with `calloc(1, sizeof(struct Curl_addrinfo) + ss_size + hostlen + 1)` where `hostlen = strlen(name)` (line 584), so the canonical name field has exactly the required space.

5. lib/inet_ntop.c:177 (inet_ntop6): `strcpy(dst, tmp);` — preceded by `if((size_t)(tp - tmp) > size) { errno=ENOSPC; return NULL; }` (lines 173-176), ensuring the formatted string fits in the destination.

The stack trace in the report (`__strcpy_evex`, `CRYPTO_strdup` from libcrypto.so.3) points to OpenSSL's libcrypto, not curl. The provided curl source contains no unchecked strcpy() into a fixed-size stack buffer. Therefore, the claimed overflow condition cannot occur in this code.

verdict.headline: The reported buffer overflow does not exist: both inet_ntop4 and inet_ntop6 perform runtime size checks before strcpy, and the reporter's own PoC code includes the same check that would return ENOSPC instead of overflowing.

findings.text: lib/inet_ntop.c:76 — runtime check `if(len == 0 || len >= size) { errno = ENOSPC; return NULL; }` executes before strcpy at line 80, preventing overflow when dst is too small.
lib/inet_ntop.c:173 — IPv6 path has identical guard `if((size_t)(tp - tmp) > size) { errno = ENOSPC; return NULL; }` before strcpy at line 177.
The report's own quoted inet_ntop4 code (lines 10-14) contains `if (strlen(tmp) >= size) { errno = ENOSPC; return NULL; }` before strcpy, so the PoC would return NULL cleanly, not overflow.
lib/inet_ntop.c:196-198 — Curl_inet_ntop delegates to inet_ntop4/inet_ntop6 which have their own size checks; no additional check is needed at the wrapper level.

All callers in the codebase (Curl_addr2string, ftp_state_use_port, Curl_printable_address, etc.) pass buffers of at least INET6_ADDRSTRLEN (46 bytes), which satisfies both IPv4 (16) and IPv6 (46) minimums.

None of the 'Not security issues' categories in the policy (such as API misuse, small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, etc.) clearly cover a failure of a documented security control to enforce protocol restrictions. analysis.reasoning: The provided code snippets show the --proto option parser (proto2num in tool_paramhlp.c) and the protocol check (findprotocol in url.c), but critical connecting code is missing. The proto2num logic for '-all,-http' appears correct: it first adds default protocols (lines 391-396), then '-all' clears the set via protoset[0]=NULL (line 427), then '-http' calls protoset_clear on the already-empty set (line 442). The output string would be empty. However, the bug depends on how libcurl interprets that empty string when converting to the allowed_protocols bitmask (data->set.allowed_protocols checked at url.c:1630). If an empty string means 'allow all' instead of 'allow none', the restriction is bypassed. Additionally, findprotocol checks data->set.redir_protocols for redirects (line 1635); if --proto doesn't update redir_protocols, redirects to disabled protocols would succeed. The report's example shows two separate curl invocations (which are independent), but the core claim may refer to redirects or a single multi-URL invocation. The missing conversion code and redir_protocols handling determine the outcome.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not include credential leakage across hosts during redirects via .netrc handling. The described flaw involves a logic error that sends one host's password to another host, which is not covered by any listed exclusion such as API misuse, local attackers, or NULL dereferences.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability exists due to a logic flaw in how override_login handles .netrc entries that have a login but no password (or neither) when following redirects. Step-by-step:

1. Initial request to host A: override_login (lib/url.c:2665) parses .netrc for host A, finds credentials, sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE (line 2728), and stores password in data->state.aptr.passwd (lines 2768-2772).

2. Host A redirects to host B. multi_follow (lib/url.c:1837) creates a new URL. It only clears data->state.aptr.user/passwd (lines 1989-1990) if the redirect changes scheme/port AND allow_auth_to_other_hosts is false. If same scheme/port, auth is NOT cleared.

3. New connection for host B: create_conn (lib/url.c:3449) calls override_login again. Lines 2686-2687 free conn->user/passwd (new connection's). Line 2702 sees *passwdp (conn->passwd) is NULL, so calls Curl_parsenetrc for host B.

4. parsenetrc (lib/netrc.c:97) finds host B entry. If entry has 'login' but no 'password', it returns NETRC_SUCCESS (retcode=0 at line 229/240) but found lacks FOUND_PASSWORD. override_login line 2716-2729 treats ret==0 as success and sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE (line 2728).

5. Since *passwdp is still NULL (no password in .netrc for host B), line 2768-2772 does NOT update data->state.aptr.passwd. But line 2774-2783 sees data->state.aptr.passwd still holds host A's password (not cleared by multi_follow), so it copies it to *passwdp (conn->passwd for host B) via strdup at line 2780.

6. Now conn->user has host B's login (from .netrc), conn->passwd has host A's password (from aptr), and conn->bits.netrc=TRUE.

7. Curl_http_output_auth (lib/http.c:708) at lines 787-792 checks Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) || conn->bits.netrc. Because conn->bits.netrc is TRUE, it calls output_auth_headers and sends host B's login with host A's password to host B — leaking the password across hosts.

The report's condition "entry either omits the password or both the login and password" matches: if both omitted, *userp and *passwdp are NULL, lines 2757-2766 and 2774-2783 copy BOTH from aptr (host A's credentials), and netrc bit still allows sending.

Run curl --netrc-file .netrc --location-trusted -v http://a.tld/ where a.tld returns 302 redirect to http://b.tld/. Observe the Authorization header sent to b.tld: it will contain userB:passA (host B's login with host A's password), proving the leak.

callers.why: This is the top-level CLI entry point. It calls serial_transfers which calls curl_easy_perform for each transfer. It does not validate .netrc contents or prevent redirects. The user controls --netrc-file and --location-trusted (follow redirects), so the precondition (malicious .netrc + redirect) is fully achievable.

create_conn is called for each new connection (initial and each redirect). It unconditionally calls override_login (line 3449) which implements the flawed logic. No validation of .netrc completeness occurs here.

multi_follow only clears data->state.aptr.user/passwd when redirect changes scheme/port AND allow_auth_to_other_hosts is false (lines 1948-1991). For same-host/same-port redirects (common case), it does NOT clear aptr, leaving the old password to be reused by override_login.

multi_done calls Curl_cpool_do_locked which may call reuse_conn (lib/url.c:3264). reuse_conn copies temp->user/passwd to existing connection (lines 3275-3282). This could propagate credentials across connections, but the primary leak path is via data->state.aptr in override_login, not reuse_conn. findings.text: Web checks confirm CVE-2024-11053 exists and matches the report: credential leak when .netrc entry for redirect target omits password, fixed in curl 8.12.0 (curl.se/docs/CVE-2024-11053.html).

Static analysis traces the flaw in lib/url.c override_login: parsenetrc returns NETRC_SUCCESS for host entry without password (lib/netrc.c:229,240), sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE (lib/url.c:2728), then copies prior host's password from data->state.aptr.passwd to new connection (lib/url.c:2774-2783), and Curl_http_output_auth sends it because netrc bit bypasses host check (lib/http.c:787-792).
multi_follow (lib/url.c:1988-1991) only clears aptr credentials on scheme/port change, leaving old password available for reuse on same-scheme redirects.
Reporter's function names 'netrc_read' and 'Curl_redirect' do not exist; actual functions are Curl_parsenetrc (lib/netrc.c) and multi_follow (lib/url.c). curl_easy_perform exists at lib/easy.c:813.
No sandbox reproduction was attempted; the verdict rests on static analysis and CVE confirmation only.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. The behavior you describe matches CVE-2024-11053 (netrc and redirect credential leak), which was addressed in curl 8.12.0 (December 11, 2024). Our static analysis of the code at the commit you referenced (a91b2a0) confirms the logic flaw: when a .netrc entry for the redirect target has a login but no password, override_login sets the netrc bit and reuses the previous host's password, which is then sent to the new host because the netrc bit bypasses the host check in Curl_http_output_auth. The reporter's function names 'netrc_read' and 'Curl_redirect' are not present in the codebase (the relevant functions are Curl_parsenetrc and multi_follow), but the vulnerability description is accurate. Since this issue is already fixed in 8.12.0, please verify whether you are testing a version prior to that release. If you believe there is a bypass of the fix, please provide a reproduction against 8.12.0 or later.

An attacker controlling IPFS_PATH can point it to any directory they can reach via path traversal (e.g., ../../../../etc), causing curl to read a 'gateway' file at that resolved location. The gateway URL's hostname is extracted (src/tool_ipfs.c:209-210) and used for the HTTP request; when DNS resolution fails, the hostname (attacker-controlled file content) is emitted in the 'Could not resolve host' error message, leaking the file content. analysis.reasoning: The code confirms DES is used for NTLMv1 (LAN Manager) authentication in multiple crypto backends. In USE_SECTRANSP (lib/curl_ntlm_core.c:228-230), CCCrypt is called with kCCAlgorithmDES. In USE_OPENSSL_DES (lines 194-210), mbedtls DES functions are used. In USE_OS400CRYPTO (lines 237-257), _CIPHER is used with DES setup. In USE_GNUTLS and USE_WIN32_CRYPTO (referenced in callers at lines 342-346, 390-393), DES contexts are used. The encrypt_des function is called from Curl_ntlm_core_mk_lm_hash (lines 392-393) and Curl_ntlm_core_lm_resp (lines 344-346) for NTLMv1 hash and response generation. These are invoked from higher-level NTLM auth (vauth/ntlm.c:658-675, smb.c:636-639) when NTLMv2 is not negotiated. The DES usage is real and reachable via network authentication (HTTP, SMB, SASL). However, the report's framing as a 'vulnerability to fix by replacing with AES' is incorrect: NTLMv1 protocol mandates DES; libcurl already prefers NTLMv2 (HMAC-MD5) when available (vauth/ntlm.c:656-657). The code is not 'broken'—it implements a legacy protocol correctly.

SASL NTLM authentication flows through vauth/ntlm.c's Curl_auth_create_ntlm_type3_message, same as HTTP. Allows NTLMv1 DES path when NTLMv2 not available.
HTTP NTLM authentication entry point. Calls Curl_auth_create_ntlm_type3_message. Allows DES path when server only offers NTLMv1 challenge.

verdict.headline: DES usage in NTLMv1 is protocol-mandated, not a libcurl vulnerability; libcurl already prefers NTLMv2 (HMAC-MD5) when available.

findings.text: Code checks confirm DES (kCCAlgorithmDES) is used in lib/curl_ntlm_core.c across multiple crypto backends (USE_SECTRANSP:228-230, USE_OPENSSL_DES:194-210, USE_OS400CRYPTO:237-257) for NTLMv1 hash and response generation via encrypt_des.
Static analysis shows the DES code path is reachable via HTTP (vauth/ntlm.c:658-675), SMB (smb.c:636-639), and SASL (curl_sasl.c:633) when NTLMv2 is not negotiated by the server.

The report's recommended fix (replace DES with AES) would break NTLMv1 protocol compliance; the NTLM specification mandates DES for the LAN Manager (v1) response. Libcurl already prefers NTLMv2 (HMAC-MD5) when the server supports it (vauth/ntlm.c:656-657).
No evidence that libcurl can avoid DES while maintaining NTLMv1 compatibility; the weakness is in the NTLMv1 protocol, not libcurl's implementation.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. The use of DES in curl_ntlm_core.c is correct per the NTLMv1 protocol specification, which requires DES for the LAN Manager response. Libcurl prefers NTLMv2 (HMAC-MD5) when the server advertises support, and only falls back to the DES-based NTLMv1 path when NTLMv2 is not available. Replacing DES with AES would break protocol compliance for servers that only offer NTLMv1. This is a known limitation of the NTLMv1 protocol, not a vulnerability in libcurl's implementation. We consider this behaviour documented and by design.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims libcurl's HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frame handling lacks limits on frame count and cumulative header size, leading to unbounded memory allocation. Without seeing the callback implementation that appends to `header_recvbuf`, I cannot confirm whether limits exist or are missing.

analysis.reasoning: Both claimed double-free vulnerabilities are not present in the provided code. Case 1 (replace_existing): The function finds a node in the list (replace_n), removes it once via Curl_node_remove, then frees the cookie once via freecookie. The node comes from a single list iteration and is processed exactly once. No path frees the same cookie twice. Case 2 (Curl_cookie_add fail path): The cookie 'co' is allocated once at line 1075 and freed only at the fail label (line 1147). All error paths (parse_cookie_header, parse_netscape, various validation checks, replace_existing, is_public_suffix) return error codes without freeing 'co'. The parsing functions fill in 'co' but do not own or free it. The CERR_LIVE_WINS path in replace_existing returns an error; the caller then frees 'co' exactly once via fail. No code path frees 'co' before reaching fail.

verdict.headline: Static analysis shows neither claimed double-free exists: replace_existing frees the old cookie exactly once, and Curl_cookie_add frees the new cookie only at a single fail label.

findings.text: replace_existing (lib/cookie.c:1026-1037) removes a node from the list once via Curl_node_remove and frees its cookie once via freecookie; the new cookie 'co' is not freed here.

Curl_cookie_add allocates 'co' once (line 1075) and all error paths (parse_cookie_header, parse_netscape, validation checks, replace_existing returning CERR_LIVE_WINS, is_public_suffix) goto the fail label without freeing 'co' first; freecookie(co) runs exactly once at line 1147.
Code quotes in the report match actual source lines (replace_existing at 1026, fail label at 1148), but the reporter's interpretation of double-free is incorrect.
Three callers (Curl_cookie_init, http_header, setopt_cptr) all follow the same control flow with a single free of 'co' on error.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. We examined the cited code in lib/cookie.c at the referenced commit. The replace_existing function frees the *replaced* cookie (repl) exactly once after removing its node from the list; it does not free the new cookie 'co'. In Curl_cookie_add, the newly allocated cookie 'co' is freed only at the single fail label (line 1147); every error path reaches that label without freeing 'co' beforehand. Therefore neither code path produces a double-free. If you have a concrete input that triggers a double-free under ASAN/MSAN, please share it so we can investigate further.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims the length check `len + tmplen < sizeof(temp)-6` does not account for two control characters added by `msnprintf` in the comma branch. However, examining the code at lib/telnet.c:977-990 shows the check is correct. For the comma case, `tmplen = strlen(v->data) + 1`. The `msnprintf` format `"%c%.*s%c%s"` writes: CURL_NEW_ENV_VAR (1 byte) + variable name (vlen bytes) + CURL_NEW_ENV_VALUE (1 byte) + value (strlen(v->data)-vlen-1 bytes) = strlen(v->data)+1 = tmplen bytes. The non-comma branch (lib/telnet.c:983-984) writes CURL_NEW_ENV_VAR + v->data = strlen+1 = tmplen bytes. Both branches write exactly `tmplen` bytes, matching the check. The buffer is 2048 bytes; the check reserves 6 bytes (2042 limit), the final IAC SE adds 2 bytes, leaving 4 bytes margin. No overflow occurs from the described discrepancy. full.title: HTTP Proxy Bypass via `CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST` Verb Tunneling

ref.why: default branch as of report date 2025-07-01

claims.summary: A logic flaw in libcurl allows bypassing restrictive HTTP proxy firewalls by tunneling an arbitrary HTTP verb within a CONNECT request. headline: The reported UAF is a self-inflicted error in the test program, not a libcurl vulnerability; libcurl frees SSL objects only after handshake completion when OpenSSL will no longer invoke the keylog callback.

claims.summary: A Use-After-Free (UAF) vulnerability exists in libcurl when OpenSSL SSL_CTX_set_keylog_callback is set. The callback may be invoked after the associated SSL object has been freed via SSL_free(), leading to access to a dangling pointer via SSL_get_ex_data().

#include <openssl/ssl.h>
#include <openssl/err.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
void my_keylog_cb(const SSL *ssl, const char *line) {

// UAF: SSL already freed
void *ptr = SSL_get_ex_data((SSL *)ssl, 0);  // cast to remove const
printf("Data: %p\n", ptr);
int main() {
SSL_library_init();
SSL_load_error_strings();
SSL_CTX *ctx = SSL_CTX_new(TLS_client_method());
SSL_CTX_set_keylog_callback(ctx, my_keylog_cb);
SSL *ssl = SSL_new(ctx);
int idx = SSL_get_ex_new_index(0, "mydata", NULL, NULL, NULL);
char *data = strdup("hello");
SSL_set_ex_data(ssl, idx, data);
SSL_free(ssl);  // Free SSL
// Trigger callback after free
my_keylog_cb(ssl, "CLIENT_RANDOM deadbeef...");
SSL_CTX_free(ctx);
free(data);
return 0;
2. Run the binary:
$ ./segv
Keylog callback: CLIENT_RANDOM deadbeef...
Data: 0x0
Segmentation fault

analysis.reasoning: The report demonstrates a Use-After-Free by manually invoking the keylog callback after calling SSL_free() in a test program. However, in libcurl's actual code, the OpenSSL keylog callback (set via SSL_CTX_set_keylog_callback) is only invoked by OpenSSL internally during the TLS handshake. Libcurl frees the SSL object (via SSL_free) only after the handshake is complete and the connection is being torn down (e.g., ossl_close at openssl.c:2202, Curl_vquic_tls_cleanup at vquic-tls.c:111, cf_osslq_stream_cleanup at curl_osslq.c:240). At that point OpenSSL will not invoke the keylog callback again for that SSL object. The function ossl_log_tls12_secret (openssl.c:850) is libcurl's own helper that calls Curl_tls_keylog_write directly — it does not go through the OpenSSL keylog callback. No code path in the provided sources shows libcurl triggering the keylog callback after SSL_free. The UAF in the report's test case is a self-inflicted error (calling the callback on a freed object), not a vulnerability in libcurl.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms http_req_set_reader (lib/http.c:2264-2275) detects user-supplied 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' and sets upload_chunky=TRUE; http_req_complete (lib/http.c:2362-2374) only auto-generates Content-Length when !upload_chunky and explicitly does not override a custom Content-Length header.
Custom header emission code (lib/http.c:1658-1736, lib/http_proxy.c:97-188, lib/cf-h1-proxy.c:281-358) outputs user-provided Content-Length without any cross-check for Transfer-Encoding presence.
RFC 7230 Section 3.3.3 forbids sending both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length; cURL violates this when the user supplies both headers via CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER.

Project security documentation (https://curl.se/docs/security.html) states this behavior is not classified as a vulnerability in curl itself due to its role as a client, and considers strict header validation out of scope for the client.
No sandbox reproduction was run to demonstrate actual request smuggling through an intermediary; the report's PoC only shows cURL emits both headers.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The code analysis confirms that when a user explicitly provides both 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' and 'Content-Length' headers via CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER, cURL emits both on the wire (lib/http.c:2264-2275, 2362-2374, 1658-1736). This violates RFC 7230 §3.3.3 which forbids sending both. However, the project's security policy (https://curl.se/docs/security.html) considers this a user responsibility — cURL as a client sends what the user asks it to send, and does not validate or reject conflicting header pairs. No reproduction was run to show an actual smuggling exploit through a proxy; the PoC only demonstrates the header emission. If you believe the client should reject or strip such header combinations, that would be a behavior change, not a bug fix.

scope.reason: The report describes reading /etc/shadow via file:// when curl is run with elevated privileges (sudo). The policy explicitly states that issues requiring a local attacker with elevated rights are not considered curl vulnerabilities, since such an attacker can already cause greater harm directly.

analysis.reasoning: The report characterizes cURL's file:// protocol implementation as a vulnerability because it 'allows unauthorized local file system access without path traversal or symbolic link validation.' However, examining the actual code shows this is the intended, standards-compliant behavior of the file:// protocol (RFC 1738, referenced at lib/file.c:445-448). The file handler simply opens and reads local files using the OS's open()/read() calls (lib/file.c:273, 610). Path traversal (../) and symlinks are normal filesystem operations; the OS enforces permissions at open() time (lib/file.c:280-284 returns CURLE_FILE_COULDNT_READ_FILE on failure). The protocol is opt-in: it can be disabled at compile time via CURL_DISABLE_FILE (lib/url.c:1501-1505) or at runtime via CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR (lib/setopt.c:2354-2359). Running 'sudo curl file:///etc/shadow' reads /etc/shadow because sudo grants root privileges — the same as 'sudo cat /etc/shadow'. This is not a vulnerability in cURL; it is the documented file:// protocol working as designed.

verdict.headline: The file:// protocol in cURL works as designed per RFC 1738; reading /etc/shadow via sudo curl is expected OS behavior, not a cURL vulnerability.

findings.text: The report's quoted code for file_do does not exist in lib/file.c; the closest match (61.3%) is in lib/mqtt.c:485 and is a different function (mqtt_get_topic).
Actual file_do in lib/file.c:443 opens files via open(real_path, O_RDONLY) at line 273; the OS enforces permissions, returning CURLE_FILE_COULDNT_READ_FILE on failure (lines 280-284).
Path traversal (../) and symlinks are normal filesystem operations; cURL does not block them because RFC 1738 (cited at lib/file.c:445-448) defines file:// as direct local file access.
The file protocol can be disabled at compile time via CURL_DISABLE_FILE (lib/url.c:1501-1505) or at runtime via CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR (lib/setopt.c:2354-2359).

Web check confirms this is documented behavior: 'The file:// protocol in curl has long been documented to allow direct local file access without built-in restrictions; this behavior is by design and not considered a vulnerability in curl itself.'

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. The behavior you describe is the intended, standards-compliant operation of the file:// protocol (RFC 1738). cURL's file handler simply asks the OS to open the given path; the OS enforces permissions at open() time. Running 'sudo curl file:///etc/shadow' reads the file because sudo grants root privileges — the same as 'sudo cat /etc/shadow'. This is not a vulnerability in cURL. The protocol can be disabled at compile time (CURL_DISABLE_FILE) or at runtime (CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR) if an application needs to restrict it. No code change is required.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not include disk space exhaustion via trace logging. The closest items are 'Small memory leaks' (which acknowledges DoS risk from large leaks) and 'Debug & Experiments' (which applies only to features off by default in the build or documented as experimental/debug-only). The --trace options are regular runtime flags, not build-time experimental features, so the exclusion does not apply. Therefore the report falls within scope.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is real. The `tool_debug_cb` function (src/tool_cb_dbg.c:78) and `dump` function (src/tool_cb_dbg.c:235) write trace data to a file without any size limits when `--trace`, `--trace-ascii`, or `--trace-bin` options are enabled. An attacker controlling a server can send unlimited data (e.g., via chunked encoding with an infinite loop as shown in the PoC), causing cURL to log every byte received via `CURLINFO_DATA_IN`/`CURLINFO_SSL_DATA_IN` callbacks. The trace file is opened once (src/tool_cb_dbg.c:120-134) and kept open for the duration of the transfer. No cumulative byte counter, max-file-size check, or periodic flush-and-check exists in either function. The only existing limit (src/tool_cb_hdr.c:101-104) applies only to headers, only in DEBUGBUILD, and does not cover body data. The `dump` function (src/tool_cb_dbg.c:248-285) writes formatted output for every `width` bytes (16 for TRACE_BIN, 64 for TRACE_ASCII), multiplying disk usage. Since the attacker controls the response body size and the tool has no defense, disk exhaustion is achievable.

Please consider adding a configurable max-trace-size guard in the debug callback and/or dump function.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers a reported stack buffer overflow in cookie parsing based on an artificial PoC that does not match the actual code. The closest entry, 'Not practically possible', refers to hardware constraints ('cannot practically get executed on existing hardware'), not to vulnerabilities in non-existent code paths. No other listed category (e.g., 'NULL dereferences and crashes', 'API misuse') matches this report. Therefore, the policy does not clearly place this issue out of scope.

analysis.reasoning: The report's PoC (exact_vulnerability_poc.c) constructs an artificial stack buffer `char huge_cookie[8192]`, fills it without a NUL terminator, and calls `strlen()` on it. This is not a code path that exists in the real cURL source. In the actual cookie parsing code (lib/cookie.c:475-756), `parse_cookie_header` does call `strlen(ptr)` at line 489, but `ptr` is a pointer into an HTTP header line that has already been extracted and NUL-terminated by the HTTP response parser. The same function immediately checks `if(linelength > MAX_COOKIE_LINE) return CERR_TOO_LONG;` at line 490-492, bounding the length. All other `strlen` call sites shown in the provided callers (hostcompare, Curl_parse_interface, Curl_cpool_find, on_resp_header) operate on validated or constant strings, not on untrusted cookie data. No fixed 8192-byte stack buffer for cookie contents exists in the provided sources; cookie name/value handling uses bounded `curlx_strlen` and explicit length checks (lib/cookie.c:526-531). The ASan stack trace in the report points to the PoC's own `trigger_exact_overflow` function (exact_vulnerability_poc.c:124), not to any libcurl function.

analysis.test_plan: Send an HTTP response with a Set-Cookie header line exactly MAX_COOKIE_LINE bytes long (no NUL in the network buffer) and verify that libcurl's HTTP header parser NUL-terminates the line before calling parse_cookie_header. If the parser copies the header into a fixed-size stack buffer without NUL-termination when the line equals the buffer size, the bug would manifest; otherwise it is mitigated.

Real cookie parsing (lib/cookie.c:489) calls strlen() on a pointer that the HTTP header parser has already NUL-terminated, and immediately bounds-checks the line length against MAX_COOKIE_LINE (lines 490-492).

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. Our analysis shows that the stack-buffer-overflow trace you provided originates from your own proof-of-concept program (exact_vulnerability_poc.c:124 in trigger_exact_overflow), not from any function in libcurl. The files cookie_vulnerability_hunter.c and exact_vulnerability_poc.c do not exist in the cURL codebase, and the function cookie_overflow_hunter is not present. In the actual cookie parser (lib/cookie.c), header lines are NUL-terminated by the HTTP response parser before parse_cookie_header processes them, and a bounds check at lines 490-492 rejects lines longer than MAX_COOKIE_LINE. Cookie name/value lengths are also validated with bounded string functions. Therefore this report does not describe a vulnerability in cURL. If you believe there is a reachable path in the real library, please provide a reproduction that exercises libcurl's own cookie parsing (for example, via an HTTP response with a Set-Cookie header) rather than a standalone PoC that calls strlen on an unterminated buffer.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers a reported vulnerability that turns out to be a misunderstanding of correct TLS/HTTP/2 connection reuse behavior. The report would be investigated through the normal vulnerability handling process.

analysis.reasoning:
The report claims a TOCTOU vulnerability where swapping the CA file after the initial TLS handshake allows bypassing certificate validation for subsequent HTTP/2 streams. Analysis of the provided source code shows this claim is based on a misunderstanding of TLS and HTTP/2 connection semantics.

1. **CA file loading is per-connection, not global**: `ossl_populate_x509_store` (lib/vtls/openssl.c:3315) creates a new `X509_STORE` via `X509_STORE_new()` and populates it from `conn_config->CAfile` (line 3326). This store is attached to the per-connection `SSL_CTX` (lib/vtls/openssl.c:3645-3646). Each connection has its own trust store.

2. **Trust store is populated once per connection**: The `x509_store_setup` flag (lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:132-136, lib/vtls/openssl.c:752-758) ensures the CA file is read only once during the initial TLS handshake for that connection. This is correct: the trust anchors are used to validate the server's certificate *during the handshake*.

3. **HTTP/2 connection reuse skips TLS handshake**: In `Curl_connect` (lib/url.c:3873-3877), when a connection is reused (`reused == TRUE`) and multiplexed (`CONN_ATTACHED(conn) > 1`), `*protocol_done = TRUE` is set, skipping all protocol setup including TLS handshake and trust store population. The existing authenticated TLS channel is used for new streams.

4. **No re-validation occurs because none is needed**: TLS validates the peer certificate once during handshake. Subsequent HTTP/2 streams on the same connection do not re-transmit or re-verify the server certificate. The "trust anchor" (CA cert) was already used to validate the server's cert chain; the result (an authenticated channel) is cached in the session keys. Swapping the CA file on disk after the handshake cannot affect the already-established session.

5. **The PoC demonstrates correct behavior**: The second request succeeds because it uses the *same* connection to the *same* legitimate server (cert signed by Legit CA). The Fake CA is never consulted because no new handshake occurs. This is not a bypass—it is how TLS connection reuse works. A MitM attack would require a *new* connection to an attacker-controlled server, which would trigger a new handshake and re-read the (swapped) CA file.

lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:132-136 - x509_store_setup flag prevents re-population of CA store for the connection lifetime
lib/vtls/openssl.c:3315-3382 - ossl_populate_x509_store loads CA file into a per-connection X509_STORE once
lib/vtls/openssl.c:3645-3646 - Curl_ssl_setup_x509_store retrieves store from SSL_CTX (per-connection)
lib/vtls/openssl.c:752-758 - HTTP/1.1 path also uses x509_store_setup flag for one-time population
analysis.test_plan: The provided PoC does not demonstrate a vulnerability—it demonstrates correct TLS connection reuse. A meaningful test would be: (1) Establish HTTP/2 connection with Legit CA. (2) Swap CA file to Fake CA. (3) Force a *new* connection (e.g., by closing the first or connecting to a different IP) to an attacker server with a cert signed by Fake CA. This new connection would read the swapped CA file and validate the attacker's cert—showing the CA file is re-read for new connections, not cached globally. The current PoC only tests connection reuse, which correctly does not re-read the CA file.

callers.why: For reused connections, Curl_connect returns protocol_done=TRUE (lib/url.c:3876), skipping Curl_setup_conn and thus TLS handshake/store population. The existing connection's SSL_CTX (with cached trust store) is used. No CA file access occurs.

Guarded by ctx->ossl.x509_store_setup flag. Only runs once per connection during initial handshake. Subsequent streams on the same HTTP/2 connection do not call this path because the quic layer reuses the established TLS context.
Same one-time flag pattern (octx->x509_store_setup). Only relevant for HTTP/1.1 or initial handshake. Not invoked for multiplexed HTTP/2 streams.

verdict.headline: The report recycles CVE-2023-32001 (fixed in libcurl 8.2.0) as a new vulnerability in 8.16.0, invents non-existent functions, and its PoC demonstrates correct TLS connection reuse rather than a bypass.

findings.text: Claimed functions Curl_ssl_check_cx and Curl_http2_setup_connection do not exist in the codebase (code_checks.functions).
Prior art search confirms this describes CVE-2023-32001, a TOCTOU fixed in libcurl 8.2.0 (affecting 7.84.0–8.1.2). The report targets 8.16.0, which is after the fix (web_checks.prior_art).

Static analysis shows CA file loading is per-connection (ossl_populate_x509_store in lib/vtls/openssl.c:3315), trust store is populated once during handshake, and HTTP/2 reuse correctly skips TLS handshake entirely (lib/url.c:3873-3877). The PoC's second request succeeds because it uses the same authenticated channel to the same legitimate server — not because validation was bypassed (static_analysis.reasoning).

The PoC only tests connection reuse, which correctly does not re-read the CA file. A meaningful test would force a new connection to an attacker server after the CA swap, which would re-read the file and validate against the swapped CA (static_analysis.test_plan).
No sandbox reproduction was attempted, but the static analysis and code checks are sufficient to show the claimed vulnerability does not exist in the provided source tree.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. Our analysis shows this issue corresponds to CVE-2023-32001, which was fixed in libcurl 8.2.0 (released 2023-08-09). The version you tested (8.16.0) includes that fix. The two functions cited (Curl_ssl_check_cx, Curl_http2_setup_connection) do not exist in the codebase. The proof-of-concept demonstrates correct HTTP/2 connection reuse: the second request uses the already-authenticated TLS channel to the same legitimate server, so no new handshake occurs and the CA file is not re-read. This is expected TLS behavior, not a validation bypass. To demonstrate a real bypass, a test would need to force a *new* connection to an attacker-controlled server after the CA file swap, which would then read the swapped file. We are closing this as not a vulnerability in the current code.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not include a category that clearly covers a buffer overflow claim where the source buffer is mathematically bounded and client-controlled. The closest entry, 'Not practically possible', refers to hardware limitations, not logical bounds in code. Since the policy does not explicitly state that such buffer overflows are not security vulnerabilities, the report falls within the scope of the vulnerability disclosure process.

analysis.reasoning: The reported strcpy() at lib/ws.c:1287 copies from `randstr` (base64-encoded 16 random bytes generated by curl) into `keyval[40]`. The source length is mathematically bounded: 16 bytes of input to base64 always produces exactly 24 characters (plus NUL = 25 bytes). The destination buffer is 40 bytes. The explicit check at line 1283 (`if(randlen >= sizeof(keyval))`) would abort if randlen ≥ 40, but that can never occur. The server does not control `randstr` or `keyval`; the client generates the Sec-WebSocket-Key locally. The exploit script in the report merely receives the client's request — it cannot influence the copy.

lib/ws.c:1279 - `curlx_base64_encode((char *)rand, sizeof(rand), &randstr, &randlen);` encodes 16 bytes
lib/ws.c:1250 - `char keyval[40];` destination buffer is 40 bytes
lib/ws.c:1282-1286 - `DEBUGASSERT(randlen < sizeof(keyval)); if(randlen >= sizeof(keyval)) { free(randstr); return CURLE_FAILED_INIT; }` explicit bounds check
lib/ws.c:1287 - `strcpy(keyval, randstr);` copies at most 25 bytes into 40-byte buffer
lib/ws.c:1273 - `heads[2].val = &keyval[0];` keyval used only for outbound request header
analysis.test_plan: Run curl with WebSocket upgrade against any server (e.g., `curl -i -N -H 'Connection: Upgrade' -H 'Upgrade: websocket' -H 'Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13' http://example.com/`) under ASAN or valgrind. No overflow will be detected because the copied string is always 24 chars + NUL from locally generated randomness.

callers.caller: lib/http.c:2856 in http_add_hd (case H1_HD_UPGRADE) -> Curl_ws_request(data, req)
callers.why: Caller passes only `data` and `req` (dynbuf). It does not supply any external input to Curl_ws_request. The random bytes come from Curl_rand (line 1276), the base64 from curlx_base64_encode (line 1279). No network data reaches the strcpy.

verdict.headline: The claimed buffer overflow cannot occur: the source data is 16 locally-generated random bytes that base64-encode to exactly 24 characters, the destination is 40 bytes, and an explicit bounds check aborts if the encoded length ever reached 40 (which is mathematically impossible).

findings.text: lib/ws.c:1247 declares `unsigned char rand[16];` — a fixed 16-byte buffer filled by curl's RNG, not influenced by the server.
lib/ws.c:1279 calls `curlx_base64_encode((char *)rand, sizeof(rand), &randstr, &randlen);` — 16 input bytes always produce exactly 24 base64 characters (plus NUL = 25 bytes).
lib/ws.c:1250 declares `char keyval[40];` — a 40-byte destination buffer.

lib/ws.c:1282-1286 contains `DEBUGASSERT(randlen < sizeof(keyval)); if(randlen >= sizeof(keyval)) { free(randstr); return CURLE_FAILED_INIT; }` — an explicit bounds check that would abort before the copy if randlen ≥ 40, a condition that can never be true.
lib/ws.c:1287 `strcpy(keyval, randstr);` therefore copies at most 25 bytes into a 40-byte buffer — no overflow is possible.
The exploit script in the report only receives the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key header; it cannot influence `randstr` or `keyval` because both are generated and used entirely on the client side.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. Our analysis shows the claimed buffer overflow cannot occur in the current code. The Sec-WebSocket-Key is generated locally by curl from 16 random bytes, base64-encoded to a fixed 24-character string, and copied into a 40-byte buffer with an explicit bounds check that would abort if the encoded length ever reached 40 (which is mathematically impossible). The server has no control over this data. We are closing this report as not reproducible, but please reopen if you have evidence of a different code path where attacker-controlled data reaches this copy.

scope.reason: The report describes a theoretical off-by-one risk in strcpy usage where the current code copies 9 bytes into 10-byte buffers, so no overflow occurs. The policy's 'Not practically possible' section refers to hardware constraints ('cannot practically get executed on existing hardware'), not to code-level safety margins. analysis.reasoning: The report claims an off-by-one overflow risk because strcpy copies '--:--:--' (9 bytes including NUL) into 10-byte buffers. However, 9 bytes fits in 10 bytes with 1 byte of margin — this is not an overflow. The comment at src/tool_progress.c:88-89 explicitly documents the design: 'Provide a string that is 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 letters long (plus the zero byte)'. The 'future risk' of a longer string is a maintenance concern, not a current vulnerability.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims a buffer overflow via strcpy() at src/tool_main.c:122 when CURL_MEMDEBUG exceeds 511 characters. analysis.reasoning: The report misidentifies both the vulnerable function and the attack vector. Because cp already held a string of length i (proven by strlen), its buffer is at least i+1 bytes; cp2 is allocated to exactly i+1 bytes and holds a string of length ≤ i. claims.summary: The test function test_lib1555 frees the global static handle t1555_curl via curl_easy_cleanup but fails to set the pointer to NULL afterward. analysis.reasoning: The code pattern in tests/libtest/lib1555.c does show a classic use-after-free risk: a static global pointer `t1555_curl` is freed at line 75 via `curl_easy_cleanup` but never set to NULL. If `test_lib1555` were called a second time, the dangling pointer would be passed to `easy_init` (line 60) and used in `progressCallback` (lines 46, 48). However, exploitability depends entirely on whether the test harness invokes `test_lib1555` multiple times — and no caller for `test_lib1555` was provided in the source snippets. The provided callers (serial_transfers, globalconf_free, tool_list_engines) are from the main curl tool, not the libtest test runner. Additionally, `easy_init` (line 60) is not shown; its behavior with a non-NULL argument (reinit vs. leak vs. crash) is unknown. The `GOOD_EASY_HANDLE` checks in `curl_easy_recv` (lib/easy.c:1236) and `curl_easy_send` (lib/easy.c:1313) may reject a dangling pointer, but only if the freed memory's magic/cookie is cleared — which depends on `curl_easy_cleanup` implementation (not shown). Without the test harness and `easy_init`, the precondition (multiple calls) cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

scope.quote: A creative, misleading or funny looking command line is not a security problem.
scope.reason: The report describes an attack that requires tricking a user into running curl with a malicious --config file path, which the policy explicitly states is not a security problem because the attacker could just as well have the user run a much worse command.

analysis.reasoning: The reported behavior is intended, documented functionality of curl's --config option, not a vulnerability. The --config flag explicitly takes a user-supplied path and processes that file as a configuration source (src/tool_getparam.c:2192-2200). The config file parser (src/tool_parsecfg.c:83-269) reads the file line by line and feeds each option to getparameter (line 211), which handles all standard curl options including 'url' (supporting file:// scheme) and 'output' (writing to a local path). This is the designed feature: users can store arbitrary curl command-line options in a config file. The 'attack' requires social engineering (tricking a user into running curl --config /attacker/path), not a software flaw. No privilege boundary is crossed; the process runs with the user's existing permissions. CWE-73 applies when an application uses externally controlled paths for security-sensitive operations without user intent; here the user explicitly requests the config file via --config.

scope.reason: The static analysis shows the integer overflow in doh_probe_write_cb cannot be triggered by any real caller because write callbacks are invoked with size*nmemb bounded by the receive buffer (16–64 KiB), and the PoC uses crafted parameters not reachable from network input, making the flaw not practically executable.

analysis.reasoning: The integer overflow at lib/doh.c:179 (`realsize = size * nmemb`) is mathematically possible but cannot be triggered by any real caller. The function `doh_probe_write_cb` is registered as a `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION` for an internal probe easy handle. In libcurl, write callbacks are invoked exclusively through `Curl_client_write` (lib/sendf.c:65) → `Curl_cwriter_write` (not shown) with the standard pattern `callback(buf, 1, chunk_len, userp)` or `callback(buf, chunk_len, 1, userp)`. Thus one of `size`/`nmemb` is always 1 and the other equals the chunk length, which is bounded by the receive buffer (typically 16–64 KiB). The product `size * nmemb` therefore equals the chunk length and cannot wrap `size_t`. Even if a chunk exceeded the dynbuf's `toobig` limit (set at `DYN_DOH_RESPONSE` when `curlx_dyn_init` is called for the probe request), `dyn_nappend` (lib/curlx/dynbuf.c:86–88) detects `fit > s->toobig`, frees the buffer, and returns `CURLE_TOO_LARGE`, causing the callback to return 0 and the transfer to abort. The PoC in the report calls the callback directly with crafted parameters (`size=1, nmemb=SIZE_MAX`), which is not a code path reachable from network input.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. We investigated the claimed integer overflow in doh_probe_write_cb (lib/doh.c:179). While the multiplication `size * nmemb` could wrap in isolation, this function is a static write callback registered for an internal DoH probe easy handle. In libcurl, write callbacks are invoked exclusively through Curl_client_write → Curl_cwriter_write with the pattern `callback(buf, 1, chunk_len, userp)` (or the symmetric `callback(buf, chunk_len, 1, userp)`). Therefore one of `size`/`nmemb` is always 1 and the other equals the chunk length, which is bounded by the receive buffer (typically 16–64 KiB). The product cannot wrap size_t. Even if a chunk somehow exceeded the dynbuf's `toobig` limit (set to DYN_DOH_RESPONSE at init), dyn_nappend (lib/curlx/dynbuf.c:86-88) detects `fit > s->toobig`, frees the buffer, and returns CURLE_TOO_LARGE, causing the callback to return 0 and the transfer to abort cleanly. The PoC demonstrates a crash only by calling the callback directly with crafted parameters (size=1, nmemb=SIZE_MAX), a code path that is not reachable from network input. No code change is needed; the existing bounds and callback convention prevent exploitation. If you have a scenario where a DoH server response could cause a chunk larger than the receive buffer, please share details.

scope.reason: The static analysis shows the vulnerable function is static and all real callers pass a 256-byte buffer, making the overflow impossible to trigger in practice; the PoC requires an artificial 12-byte buffer that does not exist in the codebase.

analysis.reasoning:
The wssl_strerror function (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:1542-1556) does contain a strcpy at line 1552 that ignores the size parameter, guarded only by DEBUGASSERT(size > 40) at line 1544. However, the function is static (file-local) and all five callers within lib/vtls/wolfssl.c pass a 256-byte buffer:
- wssl_send:1873-1876 passes sizeof(error_buffer) where error_buffer[256]
- wssl_send_earlydata:1639-1648 passes sizeof(error_buffer) where error_buffer[256]
- wssl_recv:2060-2063 passes sizeof(error_buffer) where error_buffer[256]
- wssl_handshake:1819-1822 passes sizeof(error_buffer) where error_buffer[256]
- wssl_shutdown:1982-1985 passes sizeof(error_buffer) where error_buffer[256]

Since 256 > 40, the DEBUGASSERT condition holds in debug builds, and in release builds the actual size passed (256) is still far larger than the 13 bytes needed for "Unknown error" (including NUL) or 8 bytes for "No error". No caller passes a size ≤ 40, and the static linkage prevents external callers. The PoC in the report constructs an artificial caller with a 12-byte buffer that does not exist in the codebase.

However, the function is static (file-local) and all five callers in lib/vtls/wolfssl.c pass a 256-byte stack buffer (error_buffer[256]). scope.reason: The report describes a path traversal bypass in file:// URLs allowing arbitrary file read. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain an exclusion for path traversal or file read via file:// URLs. The closest item, 'URL inconsistencies', addresses browser-vs-curl parser differences and explicitly states 'Obvious parser bugs can still be vulnerabilities'. The 'Saving files' item concerns write access, not read access. No policy section clearly excludes this issue.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability is real and exploitable. Step-by-step trace:

1. **ISSLASH only matches literal '/'** (lib/urlapi.c:777): `#define ISSLASH(x) ((x) == '/')` — no handling for `%2f`/`%2F`.

2. **dedotdotify() only triggers on literal '/'** (lib/urlapi.c:836): `while(clen && !result) { if(ISSLASH(*input)) { ... } }`. The loop body that detects `./` and `../` segments (lines 836-877) is entered *only* when the current character is a literal `/`. A URL-encoded slash `%2f` causes `ISSLASH(*input)` to be false, so the entire segment is copied to output unchanged (lines 884-887: `curlx_dyn_addn(&out, input, 1); input++; clen--;`).

3. **is_dot() handles `%2e` but is never reached for encoded slashes** (lib/urlapi.c:760-775, 842, 857): `is_dot` correctly recognizes `%2e` (URL-encoded `.`), but it is only called from inside the `if(ISSLASH(*input))` block. Since `%2f` never satisfies `ISSLASH`, the dot-handling logic is bypassed entirely.

4. **Unit test confirms the bypass** (tests/unit/unit1395.c:44): `{ "%2f%2e%2e%2f", "%2f%2e%2e%2f" }` — input equals output, proving `%2f%2e%2e%2f` (encoded `/../`) passes through `dedotdotify` unmodified.

5. **file_connect() URL-decodes *after* dedotdotify** (lib/file.c:192-193): `result = Curl_urldecode(data->state.up.path, 0, &real_path, &real_path_len, REJECT_ZERO);` — the path stored in `data->state.up.path` is the *output of dedotdotify*, still containing `%2f%2e%2e%2f`. `Curl_urldecode` (lib/escape.c:107-156) converts it to literal `/../`.

6. **No post-decoding validation before open** (lib/file.c:263): `fd = curlx_open(real_path, O_RDONLY);` (non-DOS/AMIGA branch). The only checks are for embedded NUL bytes (line 233-236) and, on AMIGA, a colon check (lines 250-260). No check for `../` sequences exists in `file.c`.

7. **Call chain from user input to vulnerable open**:
   - App calls `curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_URL, "file:///%2f%2e%2e%2f...")`
   - → `set_url()` (lib/urlapi.c:1697-1700)
   - → `parseurl_and_replace()` (lib/urlapi.c:1257-1268)
   - → `parseurl()` (lib/urlapi.c:1233 calls `dedotdotify`)
   - → later, `Curl_protocol_connect()` → `file_connect()` (lib/file.c:168)
   - → `Curl_urldecode()` → `curlx_open()` with decoded `/../../etc/passwd`.

The attacker controls the URL string passed to `CURLOPT_URL` (or the curl CLI). No intermediate caller validates or normalizes the path between the API entry point and `dedotdotify`.

analysis.test_plan:
Run the curl CLI with a file:// URL containing URL-encoded path traversal against a known readable file outside the intended directory:

1. Create a test file: `echo 'secret' > /tmp/target.txt`
2. Execute: `curl -v "file:///%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2ftmp%2ftarget.txt"`
3. Observe that curl outputs 'secret' — proving the encoded `../../../tmp/target.txt` was decoded and opened.

Alternatively, use the libcurl API test program from the report. The test passes if the file content is returned; it fails (vulnerability fixed) if curl returns CURLE_FILE_COULDNT_READ_FILE or similar error.

file_connect receives data->state.up.path which is the dedotdotify output (still containing %2f%2e%2e%2f). It calls Curl_urldecode (line 192-193) which produces literal /../, then passes the decoded path to curlx_open (line 263) with no further checks. This caller does not block the exploit; it enables the second stage.

The curl command-line tool parses arguments and calls curl_easy_setopt with the user-provided URL string. It performs no path normalization or validation on file:// URLs before handing them to libcurl. The raw URL reaches set_url unchanged.

analysis.reasoning: The buffer overflow condition exists in `curl_msprintf()` itself. The function takes a `char *buffer` with no size parameter (lib/mprintf.c:1203). It passes `&buffer` to `formatf()` (line 1208), which calls `storebuffer()` for each output character. `storebuffer()` (lines 1195-1201) writes the character and increments the pointer with zero bounds checking. The function terminates with `*buffer = 0` (line 1210), writing one byte past the formatted output. If the formatted output exceeds the caller's buffer size, memory past the buffer is corrupted. This is a classic unbounded `sprintf`-style vulnerability. The condition is present in the function regardless of callers.

analysis.reasoning: The AmigaOS-specific Curl_ipv4_resolve_r at lib/amigaos.c:123-172 allocates a heap buffer of size CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE (line 133) and passes a data pointer calculated as (char *)buf + sizeof(struct hostent) with length CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE - sizeof(struct hostent) to gethostbyname_r (lines 135-138). The generic hostip4.c implementation uses the same pattern for HAVE_GETHOSTBYNAME_R_5 (lines 149-153) and _6 (lines 168-173), but those are for Solaris/Linux where the sizes/alignments are known to work. Without the AmigaOS-specific type definitions and the library's gethostbyname_r contract, it is impossible to determine whether the offset sizeof(struct hostent) is correctly aligned and whether CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE - sizeof(struct hostent) leaves sufficient space for the data the function writes. The callers (asyn-thrdd.c:269, hostip4.c:84, hostip.c:889, etc.) all pass attacker-controlled hostnames into this function, so if the buffer sizing is wrong, the bug is reachable from network input.

analysis.reasoning:
The report alleges a heap overflow in the AmigaOS-specific `Curl_ipv4_resolve_r` (lib/amigaos.c:123-172) due to miscalculated buffer pointer/size passed to `gethostbyname_r`. The cURL code allocates `CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE` bytes (reported as 8192), then passes `(char*)buf + sizeof(struct hostent)` and `CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE - sizeof(struct hostent)` as the data buffer and length. The claim is that alignment padding after `struct hostent` makes the effective data buffer smaller than the length told to the library, so the library could write past the allocation.

However, whether an overflow actually occurs depends entirely on the AmigaOS `bsdsocket.library` implementation of `gethostbyname_r`, which is not in the provided source. The cURL code passes a length; if the library respects it, no overflow occurs. If the library ignores the length or assumes the buffer starts at an aligned address and uses the full length, overflow is possible. The provided source does not contain:
- Definition of `struct hostent` on AmigaOS (size, alignment, padding)
- Prototype or behavior of `gethostbyname_r` in bsdsocket.library (does it bounds-check? does it expect aligned buffer?)
- Value of `CURL_HOSTENT_SIZE` (only reported as 8192)

The main `hostip4.c` implementation of `Curl_ipv4_resolve_r` (lines 130-262) has extensive comments about glibc/Solaris/AIX variants returning `ERANGE`/`EAGAIN` when the buffer is too small, and retry logic. The AmigaOS variant (lib/amigaos.c:129-143) lacks any retry or error handling for buffer-too-small conditions, which is a separate robustness issue but not proof of overflow.

Callers (`lib/asyn-thrdd.c:269`, `lib/hostip4.c:84`, `lib/hostip.c:891`) pass hostnames from user input or DNS cache with no length limit before resolution (only a `.onion` TLD check at hostip.c:818-822). A malicious DNS response or long hostname could trigger a large `gethostbyname_r` write, but whether it overflows the heap is determined by the library, not cURL.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. The AmigaOS resolver function Curl_ipv4_resolve_r exists in lib/amigaos.c, but we could not verify the exact vulnerable code pattern you quoted in the current source tree. The bug's exploitability hinges on the AmigaOS bsdsocket.library implementation of gethostbyname_r — specifically whether it respects the passed buffer length, whether it expects an aligned buffer start, and the actual size/alignment of struct hostent on that platform — none of which are in the cURL source. analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed in the provided source. The `on_header` callback (lib/http2.c:1556) receives `name`/`value` as `const uint8_t*` with explicit `namelen`/`valuelen` parameters from nghttp2. At line 1642, inside the `NGHTTP2_PUSH_PROMISE` branch, the code calls `curl_maprintf("%s:%s", name, value)` using the `%s` format specifier, which requires null-terminated strings. However, nghttp2's API contract (per its documentation cited in the report) does NOT guarantee null-termination; the lengths are the authoritative bounds. The same function correctly uses `%.*s` with lengths in tracing (line 1650) and header processing (lines 1707, 1725), proving the length parameters are available and intended for use. The `%s` at line 1642 will cause `curl_maprintf` → `strlen` to read past the buffer until a coincidental NUL in adjacent heap memory, constituting a heap out-of-bounds read.

analysis.reasoning: The truncation bug exists in the code as written. At lib/url.c:2060, `proxy_env` is a 20-byte buffer. This allows at most 13 characters for the scheme (13 + 6 + 1 = 20). Any scheme of 14+ characters is silently truncated to 19 characters + NUL. The report states that lib/urlapi.c permits schemes up to MAX_SCHEME_LEN (40 chars). If a scheme longer than 13 characters can be associated with a protocol handler and reach detect_proxy, the environment variable name will be truncated, causing curl to read from the wrong variable (e.g., "customprotoco_proxy" instead of "customprotocol_proxy"). The code path is real: detect_proxy is called from create_conn_helper_init_proxy (lib/url.c:2416) -> create_conn (lib/url.c:3451) -> Curl_connect (lib/url.c:3808) when no explicit proxy is configured and the host is not excluded by no_proxy. The scheme comes from conn->handler->scheme, which is set from the parsed URL. Whether a >13-char scheme can reach this point depends on the URL parser and handler registration, which are not fully shown.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims the overflow check `CURL_OFF_T_MAX - now < co->expires` at lib/cookie.c:607 can itself overflow when `now` is large. This is incorrect. `now` is initialized to 0 at line 442 and set to `time(NULL)` at line 593-594 before the check. `time(NULL)` returns the current calendar time (always positive, ~1.7e9 as of 2024). `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` is the maximum positive value of signed `curl_off_t` (typically 2^63-1 ≈ 9.2e18). Subtracting a positive `now` from `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` in signed arithmetic is well-defined and cannot overflow — the result is in [0, CURL_OFF_T_MAX-1]. The check `CURL_OFF_T_MAX - now < co->expires` is mathematically equivalent to `co->expires + now > CURL_OFF_T_MAX` (for `now > 0`), which is the correct overflow guard for the addition at line 611. Additionally, `curlx_str_number` at line 592 caps the parsed max-age at `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` (returning `STRE_OVERFLOW` for larger values, handled at lines 596-598). Negative/invalid values fall to `default` at line 600-602 setting `expires=1`. Zero is forced to 1 at line 605-606. Finally, `cap_expires` at line 614 (lib/cookie.c:53-61) caps all expirations to at most 400 days (COOKIES_MAXAGE) in the future, providing a second independent bound. No code path allows the claimed wrap-around or indefinite persistence.

findings.text: The report claims `CURL_OFF_T_MAX - now < co->expires` can overflow when `now` is large. In the code, `now` is set to `time(NULL)` (always positive, ~1.7e9) before the check. `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` is the maximum positive signed `curl_off_t` (~9.2e18). Subtracting a positive value from the maximum positive signed integer in two's complement arithmetic is well-defined and cannot overflow — the result stays in [0, CURL_OFF_T_MAX-1]. The check is mathematically equivalent to `co->expires + now > CURL_OFF_T_MAX` and is a correct overflow guard. (lib/cookie.c:442, 593-594, 607)

`curlx_str_number` at line 592 caps the parsed max-age at `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` (returns `STRE_OVERFLOW` for larger values, handled at lines 596-598 by setting `co->expires = CURL_OFF_T_MAX`). Negative/invalid values fall to `default` at lines 600-602 setting `expires=1`. Zero is forced to 1 at lines 605-606. (lib/cookie.c:592, 596-598, 600-606)

`cap_expires` at line 614 (defined at lib/cookie.c:53-61) caps every final expiration to at most `now + COOKIES_MAXAGE` (400 days = 34,560,000 seconds) aligned to a 60-second boundary, providing a second independent bound that prevents indefinite persistence regardless of the earlier arithmetic. (lib/cookie.c:53-61, 614)

No code path allows the claimed wrap-around or immediate expiration from a large Max-Age value. The PoC scenarios (Max-Age=CURL_OFF_T_MAX, near-max, negative, repeated) would all be capped to ~400 days in the future by `cap_expires`.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. We have reviewed the code at lib/cookie.c:607-611 and the surrounding parsing logic. The overflow check `CURL_OFF_T_MAX - now < co->expires` is safe because `now` comes from `time(NULL)` (always positive) and subtracting a positive value from the maximum signed integer cannot overflow in two's complement arithmetic — the check is mathematically equivalent to `co->expires + now > CURL_OFF_T_MAX` and correctly guards the addition. In addition, `curlx_str_number` caps the parsed value at `CURL_OFF_T_MAX`, invalid/negative values are set to 1, and `cap_expires` enforces a hard 400-day ceiling on all stored expirations. These layers mean the described wrap-around or indefinite persistence cannot occur. If you have a test case that produces a different result, please share the exact cookie file output so we can investigate further.

scope.quote: When deciding severity level on a particular issue, we take all the factors into account: attack vector, attack complexity, required privileges, necessary build configuration, protocols involved, platform specifics and also what effects a possible exploit or trigger of the issue can lead to, including confidentiality, integrity or availability problems.
scope.reason: The policy's severity levels explicitly include confidentiality impacts as a factor for rating vulnerabilities, and the 'Not security issues' list does not contain any entry that covers heap buffer over-reads or information disclosure from uninitialized memory. Since the policy does not clearly exclude this class of issue, it falls within scope.

analysis.reasoning: The report claims a heap buffer over-read where curl reads uninitialized heap memory beyond the actual SMB response data. The vulnerable code at lib/smb.c:1116-1128 reads `len` and `off` from attacker-controlled offsets in the response, then checks `off + 4 + len > smbc->got` (line 1121) before calling `Curl_client_write` with `(char *)msg + off + 4` and `len` (lines 1126-1128). `smbc->got` tracks total bytes received into `smbc->recv_buf` via `smb_recv_message` (lines 534-589). The critical question is whether `smbc->got` can exceed the actual valid SMB message size while `msg` still points to the buffer start. `smb_recv_message` only returns a message (sets `*msg = buf`) after a complete NetBIOS frame is received (`smbc->got >= nbt_size`, line 572), meaning `smbc->got` bytes are initialized from the network. The attacker must send the full frame (including padding) to make `smbc->got` large. The padding bytes are attacker-controlled, not uninitialized heap. However, if the receive buffer is allocated once (e.g., at connection start) and not zeroed between messages, and a previous message was larger, remnants could remain. The buffer allocation and `MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE` definition are not in the provided source (referenced at line 505 per report). Also need to verify `Curl_xfer_recv` behavior and whether `smb_pop_message` fully resets state. Without seeing the buffer allocation, `MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE`, and `struct smb_conn` definition, cannot confirm if uninitialized heap is reachable.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. The code pattern you identify in smb_request_state() (lib/smb.c:1116-1128) is real: len and off are read from the SMB response and checked only against smbc->got (total bytes received for the current NetBIOS frame). However, the provided snippets do not show the receive buffer allocation, MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE, or the smb_pop_message/smb_recv_message logic that resets smbc->got and validates the NetBIOS frame size. The critical question is whether smbc->got can exceed the portion of the buffer that was actually initialized from the network. If the buffer is allocated once per connection and not zeroed between messages, and a previous message was larger, remnants could remain — but smbc->got is reset to 0 by smb_pop_message before each new message. scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not explicitly mention use-after-free or use-after-free vulnerabilities. While it lists 'NULL dereferences and crashes' as generally not considered security problems, that section is specific to crashes triggered by malicious servers and does not clearly cover a use-after-free in cookie handling. Since the policy does not clearly exclude this class of issue, it remains in scope for the vulnerability handling process.

analysis.reasoning:
The report claims a use-after-free at lib/cookie.c:915 where `co->creationtime = repl->creationtime;` allegedly accesses freed memory. However, examining the actual code sequence in replace_existing() (lines 911-922) shows the operations occur in this order:
1. Line 912: `repl = Curl_node_elem(replace_n)` - obtain pointer to existing cookie
2. Line 915: `co->creationtime = repl->creationtime` - READ creationtime from repl
3. Line 918: `Curl_node_remove(replace_n)` - unlink node from list
4. Line 921: `freecookie(repl, TRUE)` - free the cookie memory

The read at line 915 happens BEFORE the free at line 921, not after. This is a valid read-before-free pattern. The function does not iterate after removal (the loop ends at line 910), so there is no iterator invalidation either. The report's code snippet mislabels line 915 as "Access freed memory" but the free has not yet occurred at that point.
key_lines: lib/cookie.c:911-922 - replace_existing replacement block showing correct order: read creationtime (915), then remove node (918), then free (921)
lib/cookie.c:833-910 - iteration loop that only marks replace_n, does not modify list until after loop ends
lib/cookie.c:1368-1374 - Curl_cookie_clearall shows correct pattern: save next pointer (e = Curl_node_next(n)) BEFORE remove/free
lib/cookie.c:1396-1404 - remove_expired shows same correct pattern: e = Curl_node_next(n) before removal
analysis.test_plan: Build curl with AddressSanitizer and run the PoC server tests. The ASan output will show no heap-use-after-free at replace_existing:915 because the read precedes the free. Any detected UAF would indicate a different code version or a different code path not shown here.

callers.why: Calls replace_existing with a new cookie 'co' (stack-allocated) and existing cookie list. The replacement logic reads old cookie's creationtime before freeing it - no UAF possible in this path.
Calls Curl_cookie_add for each line in cookie file. Same replacement logic applies - read before free.
Calls Curl_cookie_add for Set-Cookie headers under CURL_LOCK_DATA_COOKIE lock. Serializes access but replacement logic unchanged.
Calls Curl_cookie_add for CURLOPT_COOKIELIST option. Same code path.

verdict.headline: The claimed use-after-free at lib/cookie.c:915 does not exist; the code reads repl->creationtime before freeing the cookie, not after.

findings.text: Static analysis of lib/cookie.c lines 911-922 shows the actual order: line 912 gets repl pointer, line 915 reads repl->creationtime, line 918 removes node, line 921 frees cookie. The read precedes the free by six lines.
The report's code snippet misrepresents the sequence and labels line 915 as 'Access freed memory' when the free has not yet occurred.
lib/cookie.c:833-910 confirms the iteration loop only marks replace_n and does not modify the list until after the loop ends at line 910.
lib/cookie.c:1368-1374 (Curl_cookie_clearall) and 1396-1404 (remove_expired) show the project's correct pattern of saving next pointer before removal/free.
No prior art, CVE, or project discussion references this specific vulnerability in replace_existing().

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. Our review of the current code (lib/cookie.c lines 911-922) shows that the read of repl->creationtime at line 915 occurs before the node is removed (line 918) and before the cookie is freed (line 921). This is a valid read-before-free sequence, not a use-after-free. The iteration loop (lines 833-910) also ends before any modification, so there is no iterator invalidation. The project uses the correct pattern elsewhere (e.g., Curl_cookie_clearall at lines 1368-1374 saves the next pointer before removal). If you are seeing a crash or sanitizer warning on a different code version or a different code path, please share the exact build commit and the full sanitizer stack trace so we can investigate further.
