asked_for: Curl_gmtime (lib/curl_gmtime.c or lib/gmtime.c) - to confirm exact failure condition for timestamp 67768036190000000+now and that no clamping/special-casing exists below TIME_T_MAX

verdict.headline: HSTS cache truncation and silent data loss when an HTTPS origin sends a max-age value that parses but exceeds struct tm's representable range, confirmed by static analysis of the code paths.

findings.text: Curl_hsts_parse() (lib/hsts.c:177) accepts max-age=67768036190000000 via curlx_strtoofft with CURL_OFF_T_MAX limit, then adds current time to form absolute expiry stored in sts->expires (lib/hsts.c:224-228).
Curl_fopen() (lib/fopen.c:59) opens the destination cache file with FOPEN_WRITETEXT mode, truncating the original file immediately before any validation or serialization occurs.

hsts_out() (lib/hsts.c:335) calls Curl_gmtime() on the absolute expiry; Curl_gmtime() (lib/parsedate.c:633-642) returns CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT when gmtime_r/gmtime returns NULL because the timestamp (~year 2.14e9) exceeds struct tm's 32-bit tm_year range on 64-bit platforms.

Curl_hsts_save() breaks the save loop on hsts_out error (lib/hsts.c:383-384), closes the temp handle, and unlinks the temp file (lib/hsts.c:390-391), leaving the original cache truncated to zero bytes.

Curl_close() (lib/url.c:411) discards the Curl_hsts_save() return value; all callers (curl_easy_cleanup, HTTP/2 pushed streams, connection cache close) propagate this discard behavior, so curl exits successfully.
GitHub issue #7720 confirms the gmtime_r overflow gap for TIME_T_MAX; the report extends this to smaller accepted timestamps outside struct tm's range.
No sandbox reproduction was run to verify the end-to-end exploit (cache file creation, malicious server response, curl invocation, cache truncation, and policy loss on reload).
The exact max-age value 67768036190000000 was not independently verified against the current time to confirm the absolute expiry exceeds gmtime representability on all 64-bit platforms.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis confirms the vulnerability chain: Curl_hsts_parse accepts a max-age value that fits in time_t but produces an absolute expiry outside struct tm's range; Curl_fopen truncates the cache file before serialization; hsts_out fails via Curl_gmtime; the save loop aborts and deletes the temp file; Curl_close discards the error. This would cause cross-origin HSTS state loss. The reproduction steps are detailed and plausible but have not been executed. Please verify the exact gmtime failure threshold for the reported max-age value on your target platforms and test the reproduction. If confirmed, the fix should address both the truncate-before-write behavior in Curl_fopen and the missing validation/clamping of expires values before serialization.

title: secure cookie attribute bypass with tab
headline: The strparse-based cookie parser in lib/cookie.c fails to skip HTAB (0x09) as whitespace before attribute names, causing the Secure flag to be silently dropped and HTTPS-only cookies to leak over HTTP — a regression introduced in curl 8.13.0.

full.title: secure cookie attribute bypass with tab

ref.why: commit linked in the report (1aea05a6c26)

claims.summary: A Set-Cookie header using HTAB (horizontal tab) before the Secure attribute causes curl to silently drop the Secure flag, leaking HTTPS-only cookies over plaintext HTTP. The new strparse-based cookie parser in lib/cookie.c does not skip HTAB as whitespace before attribute names, unlike the previous parser.
repro_steps: Build curl at commit c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056 or any version from 8.13.0 onward with OpenSSL support

Start an HTTP server on port 8080 echoing back the Cookie header
Set the HTAB cookie: curl -ks --noproxy '*' --resolve test.invalid:8443:127.0.0.1 -c /tmp/htab.jar https://test.invalid:8443/htab
Make follow-up HTTP request: curl -sS --noproxy '*' --resolve test.invalid:8080:127.0.0.1 -b /tmp/htab.jar http://test.invalid:8080/
Observe that the response body contains sid=HTAB_SECRET proving Secure flag was dropped
Inspect cookie jar — fourth field (Secure flag) for HTAB cookie will be FALSE

scope.reason: The report describes a cookie parsing bug where a horizontal tab (HTAB) before the Secure attribute causes curl to drop the Secure flag, potentially leaking HTTPS-only cookies over HTTP. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers malformed header parsing or cookie attribute handling bugs. The closest item, 'API misuse', addresses applications using the API in undocumented ways, not server-sent header parsing. No policy section explicitly excludes this class of issue.

analysis.reasoning: The bug occurs in `parse_cookie_header` (lib/cookie.c:494-595). The do/while loop parses cookie attributes separated by ';'. After consuming a ';' via `Curl_str_single(&ptr, ';')` in the loop condition (line 595 in the first snippet, line 494 in the second), `ptr` points at the next byte. If that byte is HTAB (0x09), the next iteration calls `Curl_str_cspn(&ptr, &name, ";\t\r\n=")` (line 499). Since HTAB is in the reject set, `strcspn` returns length 0, `Curl_str_cspn` returns failure (STRE_SHORT), the `if` block is skipped, and `Curl_str_single(&ptr, ';')` in the while condition fails because the current byte is HTAB, not ';'. The loop exits, leaving the 'Secure' attribute unparsed. The cookie is stored with `secure=FALSE` (default). The previous parser had `while(ISBLANK(*ptr)) ptr++;` before each attribute; this blank-skipping was lost in the strparse conversion. `Curl_str_passblanks` (mentioned in report) is not called here.

Then make an HTTP (not HTTPS) request to the same host with -b using that jar. Observe that the cookie is sent over plaintext HTTP (response body contains sid=SECRET), proving Secure flag was dropped. Control: same with 'Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET; Secure' (space) — cookie should not be sent over HTTP.

callers.why: Extracts value after 'Set-Cookie:' and passes it directly to Curl_cookie_add with secure_context derived from connection (HTTPS=TRUE). No validation or normalization of whitespace before attributes. The server controls the exact header bytes.

Calls parse_cookie_header with the raw header line pointer. No pre-processing that would skip HTAB. The 'secure' parameter is TRUE for HTTPS, but the bug prevents the Secure attribute from being parsed, so co->secure remains FALSE.
Allows injecting a raw 'Set-Cookie:' line via CURLOPT_COOKIELIST. The line is passed verbatim to Curl_cookie_add. An attacker controlling a cookie file could embed HTAB before Secure.

verdict.headline: The strparse-based cookie parser in lib/cookie.c fails to skip HTAB (0x09) as whitespace before attribute names, causing the Secure flag to be silently dropped and HTTPS-only cookies to leak over HTTP — a regression introduced in curl 8.13.0.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms the bug in parse_cookie_header (lib/cookie.c:494-595): the do/while loop consumes ';' via Curl_str_single in the while condition but does not skip whitespace before the next Curl_str_cspn call. When the next byte is HTAB (in the reject set ";\t\r\n="), strcspn returns 0, the if block is skipped, and the loop exits because the while condition fails on HTAB. The Secure attribute is never parsed; co->secure remains FALSE (default).

The previous parser (pre-1aea05a6c26) had `while(ISBLANK(*ptr)) ptr++;` before each attribute, which correctly skipped HTAB. This blank-skipping was lost in the strparse conversion. Curl_str_passblanks exists but is not called here.

Callers allow the malicious header to reach the vulnerable code: lib/http.c:3243-3262 (http_header) passes the raw Set-Cookie value to Curl_cookie_add with secure_context=TRUE for HTTPS; lib/cookie.c:1077-1078 (Curl_cookie_add) calls parse_cookie_header with no pre-processing; lib/setopt.c:1908-1911 (setopt_cptr CURLOPT_COOKIELIST) also passes raw lines.
No sandbox reproduction was executed to demonstrate the cookie leaking over HTTP in practice.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis confirms the regression: the strparse conversion dropped the whitespace-skipping that the old parser had before each attribute name. HTAB (0x09) is valid OWS per RFC 6265 and HTTP grammar, so the parser should treat it as whitespace. The suggested fix — adding Curl_str_passblanks(&ptr) after the ';' is consumed and before Curl_str_cspn parses the next attribute name — is sound. A regression test comparing ';\tSecure' against '; Secure' and verifying neither cookie is returned for an HTTP URL should be added. Please provide a reproducer run if possible, but the code evidence is strong.

title: stale SigV4 headers sent unintended

scope.reason: The report describes a bug where setting CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 to NULL (a documented way to disable AWS SigV4 auth) returns success but fails to clear the CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 bit, causing stale Authorization headers to be sent on subsequent requests. None of the 'Not security issues' categories cover authentication state bugs or failure to clear auth bits when an option is disabled. The closest category, 'API misuse', does not apply because the API usage (setting to NULL) is documented and returns CURLE_OK, indicating it is a supported operation.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is in lib/setopt.c:2061-2072. When CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 is set to NULL, Curl_setstropt (lib/setopt.c:81-89) clears STRING_AWS_SIGV4 via CURL_EASY_STR_SET. However, the subsequent check at line 2070 only executes the 'then' branch when the string is non-empty: `if(CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4)) s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4;`. There is no 'else' branch to clear the CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 bit from s->httpauth. This contrasts with CURLOPT_HTTPSIG_ALGORITHM at lib/setopt.c:1069-1072 which correctly does `if(arg) s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG; else s->httpauth &= ~CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG;`. On the next curl_easy_perform(), the stale httpauth bit is copied into data->state.authhost.want (per report, lib/transfer.c:505). pickoneauth in lib/http.c:376-378 sees CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 in avail and selects it. Curl_output_aws_sigv4 (lib/http_aws_sigv4.c:1155) is called, which invokes parse_sigv4_params (lib/http_aws_sigv4.c:820-821). There, `const char *line = CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4);` returns empty, so it falls back to `line = "aws:amz"` and derives region/service from the hostname, producing a valid Authorization header with retained credentials.

Set CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 to explicit provider:region:service (e.g., "aws:amz:us-east-1:s3"). Perform request to test server, verify Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 header with configured scope. Set CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 to NULL, verify CURLE_OK. Change URL to different host/path. Perform second request. Observe that Authorization header is still sent (vulnerable) vs absent (fixed). callers.why: This is the direct handler for CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4. It calls Curl_setstropt with the user-provided ptr (which can be NULL). It then checks CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4) which returns false after NULL clear, so the httpauth bit is never cleared. No validation or cleanup occurs here.
Curl_setstropt faithfully stores NULL/empty string via CURL_EASY_STR_SET. It does not touch httpauth bits. Its contract is only string storage.

The outermost caller passes NULL explicitly. The API documents that NULL disables the feature. The bug is that the implementation does not honor this contract. No caller in the chain prevents the stale bit from persisting.

verdict.headline: Setting CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 to NULL clears the parameter string but leaves the CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 bit set in httpauth, causing stale SigV4 headers on reused handles.

findings.text: lib/setopt.c:2068-2071 shows the handler for CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 calls Curl_setstropt (which clears STRING_AWS_SIGV4 on NULL) but only sets s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 when the string is non-empty; no else branch clears the bit.
lib/setopt.c:1069-1072 shows the correct pattern for CURLOPT_HTTPSIG_ALGORITHM: if(arg) s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG; else s->httpauth &= ~CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG;

Static analysis traces the stale bit: lib/transfer.c copies data->set.httpauth to data->state.authhost.want; lib/http.c pickoneauth selects AWS_SIGV4 when the bit is present; lib/http_aws_sigv4.c:820 parse_sigv4_params falls back to "aws:amz" when STRING_AWS_SIGV4 is empty, producing a valid Authorization header with retained credentials.
The documented behavior in docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4.md states: "Set it to NULL to disable its use again." The implementation does not honor this contract.
No sandbox reproduction was run; the verdict rests on code inspection and static analysis alone.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report identifies a logic bug in lib/setopt.c:2068-2071 where CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4's handler fails to clear the CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4 bit when the option is set to NULL, unlike the correct pattern used for CURLOPT_HTTPSIG_ALGORITHM at lines 1069-1072. The stale bit persists in data->set.httpauth, gets copied to authhost.want on the next perform, and causes Curl_output_aws_sigv4 to generate an Authorization header using fallback parameters. The suggested fix (adding an else branch to clear the bit) matches the established pattern in the same file. A reproduction per the report's steps would confirm the behavior, but the code evidence is consistent and the claim aligns with the documented API contract.

scope.reason: The report describes a certificate validation bypass caused by a caching bug in the wolfSSL backend, where a cached CA store is incorrectly reinstalled after a user-provided callback replaces the trust store. This issue is not covered by any of the explicit exclusions in the 'Not security issues' section (e.g., it is not a memory leak, API misuse, experimental feature, NULL dereference, etc.), and the policy's list is described as incomplete but does not contain a category that clearly encompasses this type of logic flaw.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is confirmed by tracing the flag `wssl->x509_store_setup` across the call chain. In `Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store` (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:563-610), the flag is never set. It is only set inside `populate_x509_store` (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:440), which runs only on cache misses (line 598) or non-cacheable paths (line 606). On a cache hit (lines 584-587), the cached store is installed but the flag remains FALSE. Later, `wolfssl_connect_step2` (line 1076-1082) and `Curl_vquic_tls_before_recv` (lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:289-293) both check `!backend->x509_store_setup` and call `Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store` again. Because the flag is still FALSE, the second call re-enters the cache-hit branch (line 584) and reinstalls the cached store via `wolfSSL_CTX_set_cert_store`, overwriting the callback's store. No caller sets the flag after the callback returns, and no caller validates the store against the callback's choice.

analysis.test_plan: Build curl with wolfSSL, enable CA caching (CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT > 0). First request: no SSL_CTX_FUNCTION, use CA A to populate cache. Second request: new connection, set CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION callback that replaces store with CA B only. Target server presents cert signed by CA A. Vulnerable build accepts (cache hit reinstalls CA A); fixed build rejects (callback's store B is authoritative).

callers.why: Calls Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store before the SSL_CTX_FUNCTION callback runs. At this point x509_store_setup is FALSE (new backend struct), so the cache-hit path runs and installs cached store A. The callback then replaces it with store B, but the flag remains FALSE.

After ClientHello, checks !backend->x509_store_setup (still FALSE) and calls Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store again. The cache-hit condition still matches (cached_store exists, criteria met, refcount ok), so it reinstalls cached store A, overwriting the callback's store B.
For QUIC, same pattern: checks !ctx->wssl.x509_store_setup and calls setup. Flag is never set on cache hits, so the reinstalls happens here too if the handshake path reaches this point.

verdict.headline: Static analysis confirms the logic bug: x509_store_setup flag is not set on CA cache hits, allowing cached store to overwrite CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION's replacement during handshake.

findings.text: Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:563) installs cached store on hit (lines 584-587) but never sets x509_store_setup flag; flag only set in populate_x509_store (line 440) which runs only on cache misses (line 598).
wolfssl_connect_step1 (line 838) calls setup before SSL_CTX_FUNCTION callback — cache hit installs store A, flag stays FALSE; callback replaces with store B; flag still FALSE.

wolfssl_connect_step2 (line 1080) and Curl_vquic_tls_before_recv (lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:290) both check !x509_store_setup and call setup again; cache-hit condition still true, so cached store A reinstalled, overwriting callback's store B.
No sandbox reproduction executed; the bug depends on runtime callback behavior and cache state which static analysis cannot fully validate.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis traces the flag lifecycle and confirms the report's logic: on a CA cache hit, Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store installs the cached store but leaves x509_store_setup FALSE. The SSL_CTX_FUNCTION callback then replaces the store, but subsequent callers (wolfssl_connect_step2 and Curl_vquic_tls_before_recv) see the flag still FALSE and re-run the cache-hit path, reinstalling the cached store and discarding the callback's choice. Function names in the report (wssl_populate_x509_store, wssl_connect_step1) differ slightly from the actual symbols (populate_x509_store, wolfssl_connect_step1), but the code paths match. A reproduction would strengthen this to CONFIRMED; until then, the evidence strongly supports the claim. Please verify the fix (setting x509_store_setup in Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store before return) against the callers listed.

scope.reason: The report describes a bypass of SSH host verification (--knownhosts/--hostpubsha256) when redirecting from a non-SSH protocol to SFTP/SCP. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers this scenario; none of the listed exclusions (API misuse, legacy dependencies, weak algorithms, etc.) match a redirect-induced bypass of a documented security feature.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed. In `src/config2setopts.c:201-202`, `ssh_setopts()` returns immediately when `use_proto` (derived from the initial command-line URL) is not `proto_scp` or `proto_sftp`. This means `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, and `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5` are never set on the easy handle for an initial HTTPS URL. When libcurl follows a redirect to SFTP (allowed by `--proto-redir +sftp`), it reuses the same easy handle but does not re-run `config2setopts()`. The SSH connection code in `lib/vssh/libssh.c:2650-2662` and `lib/vssh/libssh.c:474+` only enforces host verification if `data->set.str[STRING_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS]`, `STRING_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, or `STRING_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5` are set — which they are not, because `ssh_setopts()` bailed out early. Verbose output explicitly reports `SSH: no knownhosts file configured` on the redirected connection, confirming the bypass.
key_lines: src/config2setopts.c:201-202 - early return prevents SSH options from being installed for non-SSH initial URLs
src/config2setopts.c:210-215 - SSH host key verification options (MD5, SHA256) only set inside the guarded block
src/config2setopts.c:231-232 - CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS only set inside the guarded block
lib/vssh/libssh.c:2650-2662 - myssh_connect() only configures knownhosts if data->set.str[STRING_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS] is set
lib/vssh/libssh.c:474-546 - ssh_check_fingerprint() only verifies SHA256/MD5 if data->set.str[STRING_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256/MD5] are set
src/config2setopts.c:955 - config2setopts() calls ssh_setopts() once during initial setup, not on redirect
analysis.test_plan: Build curl with SSH (libssh2) and HTTPS support. Start an SFTP server with a known host key and a test file. Create a known_hosts file with a deliberately wrong key for that host. Start an HTTPS server that redirects (3xx Location) to the SFTP file. Run: `curl --location --proto-redir +sftp --knownhosts wrong_known_hosts https://https-server/redirect`. Observe that curl follows the redirect, downloads the file, and reports success despite the mismatched known_hosts. Verify with `-v` that the SFTP connection logs 'SSH: no knownhosts file configured'. Repeat with `--hostpubsha256` set to a wrong value. Confirm direct SFTP access with the same wrong known_hosts fails as expected.

callers.why: Calls ssh_setopts() with use_proto derived from the initial URL only. For an HTTPS URL, use_proto is proto_https, triggering the early return at line 201-202. No SSH options are installed. Redirect handling does not reinvoke config2setopts().
Calls config2setopts() once per transfer setup. The initial URL scheme is fixed at this point; redirects are handled later inside libcurl's multi-state machine without re-running option setup.
Outermost entry point for a transfer. It initiates the URL list and calls create_single(). The initial URL determines use_proto; any redirect to SFTP occurs after this setup phase.

verdict.headline: ssh_setopts() early return bypasses SSH host verification on HTTPS-to-SFTP redirects

findings.text: src/config2setopts.c:201-202 contains the early return guard `if(use_proto != proto_scp && use_proto != proto_sftp) return CURLE_OK;` which prevents SSH options from being installed when the initial URL is not SCP/SFTP.

SSH host verification options (CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS at line 231-232, CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256/MD5 at lines 210-215) are only set inside the guarded block, so they are never applied for an initial HTTPS URL.

libcurl's SSH connection code (lib/vssh/libssh.c:474-546, lib/vssh/libssh.c:2650-2662) only enforces host verification if the corresponding easy-handle strings are set, which they are not because ssh_setopts() bailed out early.
Verbose output on a redirected SFTP connection would explicitly report 'SSH: no knownhosts file configured', confirming the bypass.
No sandbox reproduction was run to confirm the exploit works end-to-end with a live HTTPS-to-SFTP redirect and mismatched known_hosts.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The code analysis confirms the reported logic bug: ssh_setopts() returns early for non-SSH initial URLs, so CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS, CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256, and CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5 are never set on the easy handle. When libcurl follows a redirect to SFTP (allowed by --proto-redir +sftp), it reuses the same handle without re-running config2setopts(), so the SSH connection proceeds without the user's requested host-key verification. The guard exists at src/config2setopts.c:201-202 in the provided source tree. A sandbox reproduction would be needed to confirm the exploit works in practice, but the code path and the verbose log message 'SSH: no knownhosts file configured' strongly support the claim. This appears to be a distinct variant from CVE-2026-12064 (which addressed --proto-default with schemeless URLs) and remains unfixed in the current code.

title: FTP connection reuse inherits client-certificate
headline: FTP connection pooling allows a CURLUSESSL_NONE handle to inherit a prior handle's client certificate via a STARTTLS-upgraded control connection without a new TLS handshake or FTP login.

ref.why: commit linked in the report (4ff212f8ed32)

claims.summary: A transfer configured with CURLUSESSL_NONE can reuse a pooled FTP control connection that a previous handle upgraded with STARTTLS and authenticated using a client certificate, inheriting the first handle's certificate identity without a new TLS handshake or FTP login.

code_quotes.code: When an existing connection has TLS (via STARTTLS), compare client-certificate configuration even when the new handle does not itself request TLS (may_tls = false). At minimum, url_match_ssl_config() should also gate on whether the pooled connection already has TLS, not only on whether the new handle wants TLS.

scope.reason: The report describes FTP connection reuse inheriting a client certificate from a prior TLS-upgraded connection. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any category that clearly covers this scenario (e.g., connection pooling, TLS reuse, or certificate identity inheritance). No quoted sentence excludes this class of issue.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed by tracing the connection-matching logic. Three independent checks align to allow a CURLUSESSL_NONE handle to reuse a CURLUSESSL_CONTROL connection:

1. **url_match_ssl_use** (lib/url.c:800-819) permits reuse because FTP sets PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE. When the needle (new handle) is plain ftp:// (no PROTOPT_SSL) but the pooled connection is SSL-upgraded, line 811-813 checks `m->needle->scheme->flags & PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE` and same protocol family — both true for FTP — so it returns TRUE.

2. **url_match_ssl_config** (lib/url.c:982-994) only compares SSL parameters when `((m->needle->scheme->flags & PROTOPT_SSL) || m->may_tls)` is true. For CURLUSESSL_NONE, `may_tls` is set to `data->set.use_ssl > CURLUSESSL_NONE` (lib/url.c:1252), which is false. The needle has no PROTOPT_SSL. Thus the condition at line 986 is false and `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match` (which compares clientcert at vtls.c:212) is never called.

3. **ftp_conns_match** (lib/ftp.c:4452-4473) only rejects when `nftpc->use_ssl > cftpc->use_ssl` (line 4468). With enum ordering NONE=0, TRY=1, CONTROL=2, a new handle with NONE (0) vs pooled CONTROL (2) gives 0>2=false, so it passes. The reverse direction (CONTROL->NONE) would be rejected, but the vulnerable direction is allowed.

Result: the second handle attaches to the first handle's TLS-upgraded control connection without a new handshake or client-cert comparison, inheriting the authenticated FTP session.

lib/vtls.c:212 - Curl_ssl_conn_config_match compares clientcert, but never reached for CURLUSESSL_NONE

Using a shared multi-handle pool: (1) Add easy handle A with CURLOPT_USE_SSL=CURLUSESSL_CONTROL and privileged cert; perform transfer — verify success and privileged cert logged. (2) Remove handle A, keep pool. Add easy handle B with CURLOPT_USE_SSL=CURLUSESSL_NONE and no cert; perform transfer — observe reuse (CURLINFO_NUM_CONNECTS unchanged) and privileged cert identity still logged (vulnerable). (3) Repeat with CURLOPT_FRESH_CONNECT — new connection, unprivileged cert, access denied (control). (4) Repeat with explicit TLS + unprivileged cert — new connection, unprivileged identity, access denied (control).

The application controls the sequence: first handle with CONTROL+cert, second with NONE+no cert. It provides the vulnerable input. No validation occurs at this layer.

verdict.headline: FTP connection pooling allows a CURLUSESSL_NONE handle to inherit a prior handle's client certificate via a STARTTLS-upgraded control connection without a new TLS handshake or FTP login.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms the vulnerable logic path: url_match_ssl_use (lib/url.c:800-819) permits SSL reuse for FTP via PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE; url_match_ssl_config (lib/url.c:982-994) gates SSL-config comparison on (PROTOPT_SSL || may_tls), both false for CURLUSESSL_NONE (may_tls set at lib/url.c:1251-1252); ftp_conns_match (lib/ftp.c:4452-4473, line 4468) only rejects when needle.use_ssl > pooled.use_ssl, allowing CONTROL(2) -> NONE(0) reuse; Curl_ssl_conn_config_match (lib/vtls.c:212) compares clientcert but is never reached.

CVE-2016-5420 is documented at https://curl.se/docs/vuln-7.8.html as 'Reusing connections with wrong client cert' in curl 7.50.0+, matching the described issue where a pooled FTP control connection reuses a client certificate from a prior STARTTLS-upgraded handle without a new TLS handshake or FTP login.

No sandbox reproduction was executed; the verdict rests on static analysis and the prior CVE. A live test with an FTP server requiring client certificates and a shared multi-handle pool would confirm the inheritance behavior.

The report's quoted code snippets for lib/url.c and lib/ftp.c do not match the actual source (verdict: not_in_codebase), but the static analysis locates the equivalent logic at different line numbers and confirms the claim holds in the real code.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis traces a complete connection-matching path that allows a CURLUSESSL_NONE handle to attach to a pooled FTP control connection previously upgraded with STARTTLS and authenticated with a client certificate. The key points are: (1) FTP sets PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE, so url_match_ssl_use permits reuse of an SSL-upgraded connection for a plain ftp:// scheme. (2) For CURLUSESSL_NONE, may_tls is false, so url_match_ssl_config skips the client-certificate comparison (Curl_ssl_conn_config_match is never called). (3) ftp_conns_match only rejects when the new handle's use_ssl value is greater than the pooled connection's; with enum ordering NONE=0, TRY=1, CONTROL=2, a new NONE handle passes against a pooled CONTROL connection. This matches the previously fixed CVE-2016-5420. A reproduction with an FTP server that logs client-certificate identity per control connection would confirm the inheritance. The suggested fix — comparing client-certificate configuration whenever the pooled connection already has TLS, regardless of the new handle's may_tls — aligns with the analysis.

title: server-set cookie erases cookie jar
headline: Code analysis confirms a remote server can poison a shared Netscape cookie jar causing CURLE_TOO_LARGE on reload and destructive cleanup that erases all cookies.

ref.why: default branch as of report date 2026-08-27

claims.summary: A remote HTTP server can set a cookie that curl accepts and writes to a Netscape cookie jar but cannot reload. On the next invocation using the same path for --cookie and --cookie-jar, curl fails with CURLE_TOO_LARGE (100) before connecting, then cleanup replaces the jar with an empty 131-byte header, deleting cookies for unrelated domains.
claims.claimed_version: curl 8.18.0 through 8.21.0, plus affected 8.22.0 prerelease/development versions

code_quotes.code:
ci->running = TRUE;
/* always set */
/* parse_cookie_header() accepts a Set-Cookie value up to MAX_COOKIE_LINE (5000) bytes. */
Do not set ci->running = TRUE when cookie_load() fails, so cleanup cannot overwrite a jar from an incomplete load.

Make the accepted in-memory cookie limit consistent with the maximum serialized Netscape record that the loader can consume (either check the serialized length in get_netscape_format() or increase the dynbuf limit to account for the added fields).

repro_steps: 1. Build an affected curl release, starting with 8.18.0, with HTTP cookie support enabled.
2. Start two HTTP virtual hosts or test servers representing an attacker-controlled domain and an unrelated victim domain.
3. Have the victim host set a normal persistent cookie and save it to a Netscape-format cookie jar.
4. Contact the attacker-controlled host while using the same file as both cookie input and cookie-jar output.
5. Make the attacker response set a cookie that is accepted by curl's HTTP cookie parser but whose fully serialized Netscape record is one byte larger than the cookie-jar loader can consume.

6. Construct the boundary using a long but accepted cookie name or value plus a long Path attribute, accounting for the domain, flags, expiry, separators, newline, and terminating NUL added during serialization and reload.
7. Confirm that curl accepts the attacker cookie, completes the request, and writes a 4999-byte cookie record to the jar alongside the unrelated victim cookie.
8. Preserve a copy of this poisoned jar for a read-only control and record the number of requests received by the victim server.
9. Start a new curl transfer to the victim domain with the poisoned file configured as both cookie input and cookie-jar output.
10. Observe that curl fails with CURLE_TOO_LARGE before connecting because the 4999-byte record, newline, and terminating NUL exceed the loader's 5000-byte dynbuf limit.
11. Confirm that the victim server received no new request.
12. Inspect the cookie jar after curl cleanup.
13. Observe the destructive result: curl has replaced the original jar with only its standard header, deleting the attacker record and all unrelated victim cookies.
14. Repeat the reload using the preserved copy only as cookie input, without configuring cookie-jar output.
15. Confirm that loading still fails with CURLE_TOO_LARGE but the input file remains unchanged, isolating the deletion to cleanup persistence.
16. Create a boundary control in which the attacker cookie serializes to 4998 bytes instead of 4999 bytes.
17. Repeat the same-file load and save operation and confirm that the shorter record reloads successfully, the victim request occurs, and the cookie jar remains populated.
18. Confirm a fix by ensuring a failed cookie load does not mark the store as safe to persist and by making accepted in-memory cookie limits consistent with serialized reload limits.
19. Repeat the 4999-byte test and verify that curl may reject the transfer but never overwrites the original cookie jar from a partially loaded store.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a section that clearly covers a remote server causing cookie jar deletion via an oversized cookie that is accepted on set but fails on reload. The closest section ('NULL dereferences and crashes') discusses crashes and NULL dereferences, not data loss from cookie handling errors, and requires 'nothing worse' — whereas this report describes deletion of cookies for unrelated domains.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed through code analysis. 1) `parse_cookie_header` (lib/cookie.c:604-606) accepts HTTP Set-Cookie header lines up to `MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000) bytes. 2) `get_netscape_format` (lib/cookie.c:1487-1510) serializes cookies to Netscape format using `curl_maprintf` with no length limit, adding domain, path, flags, expiry, tabs, and name/value — a cookie accepted at ~5000 bytes can serialize to 4999 bytes. 3) `cookie_load` (lib/cookie.c:1178) initializes a dynbuf with `MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000); `Curl_get_line` (lib/curl_get_line.c:50-63) retains or appends a newline and the dynbuf limit includes the NUL terminator, so the maximum reloadable payload is 4998 bytes before newline. A 4999-byte record plus newline exceeds the limit and `Curl_get_line` returns `CURLE_TOO_LARGE`. 4) Despite the error, `cookie_load` unconditionally sets `ci->running = TRUE` at line 1211. 5) `Curl_pretransfer` (lib/transfer.c:529) propagates the error and aborts before connecting. 6) Cleanup via `Curl_close` (lib/url.c:254) → `Curl_flush_cookies` → `cookie_output` (lib/cookie.c:1574) sees `ci->running == TRUE` and atomically replaces the jar with the partially loaded (empty) store, deleting all cookies. No caller validates the serialized length or prevents the running flag on load failure.

verdict.headline: Code analysis confirms a remote server can poison a shared Netscape cookie jar causing CURLE_TOO_LARGE on reload and destructive cleanup that erases all cookies.

findings.text: parse_cookie_header (lib/cookie.c:604-606) accepts HTTP Set-Cookie lines up to MAX_COOKIE_LINE (5000) bytes.

get_netscape_format (lib/cookie.c:1487-1510) serializes cookies with curl_maprintf, adding domain/path/flags/expiry/tabs, with no length limit; a ~5000-byte accepted cookie can serialize to 4999 bytes.

cookie_load (lib/cookie.c:1178) initializes a dynbuf with MAX_COOKIE_LINE (5000); Curl_get_line (lib/curl_get_line.c:50-63) retains/appends a newline and the dynbuf limit includes the NUL terminator, so maximum reloadable payload is 4998 bytes before newline — a 4999-byte record triggers CURLE_TOO_LARGE.
cookie_load unconditionally sets ci->running = TRUE at lib/cookie.c:1211 even after a load error.
Curl_pretransfer (lib/transfer.c:529-533) propagates the error and aborts before connecting, but does not reset ci->running.

Curl_close (lib/url.c:254) → Curl_flush_cookies → cookie_output (lib/cookie.c:1574) sees ci->running == TRUE and atomically replaces the jar with the partially loaded (empty) store, deleting all cookies.
The HTTP cookie entry path (lib/http.c:3721 → Curl_cookie_add → parse_cookie_header) accepts the malicious cookie with no check on serialized Netscape length.
Sandbox reproduction was not run; the verdict is based on static analysis alone.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. Static analysis of the cited code (lib/cookie.c, lib/curl_get_line.c, lib/transfer.c, lib/url.c, lib/http.c) confirms the logic you describe: the HTTP parser accepts cookies up to 5000 bytes, serialization can produce a 4999-byte Netscape record, but the loader's 5000-byte dynbuf (which includes the NUL terminator and retains a newline) can only reload 4998 bytes of payload. On load failure, cookie_load still sets ci->running = TRUE (line 1211), so cleanup via Curl_close → cookie_output overwrites the jar with an empty store. The call chain from Curl_pretransfer through Curl_close does not clear the running flag on error. This appears to be a genuine bug. scope.reason: The report describes a certificate parsing flaw in the wolfSSL backend that allows bypassing public-key pinning (CURLOPT_PINNEDPUBLICKEY) by crafting a malicious certificate with manipulated validity length fields. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' categories cover this type of TLS certificate validation bypass: it is not a memory leak, never-ending transfer, API misuse, local-only attack, debug/experimental feature, test code, URL inconsistency, command-line visibility issue, busy-loop, file-saving issue, user-tricking scenario, terminal escape issue, NULL dereference/crash, legacy dependency, weak algorithm, CRLF injection, or non-released code. The policy does not clearly exclude this class of vulnerability.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability exists in curl's Curl_parseX509() (lib/vtls/x509asn1.c) which is used by the wolfSSL backend to re-parse the peer certificate DER for public-key pinning verification after the TLS handshake. The parser extracts the subjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) by sequentially parsing the TBSCertificate structure: version, serialNumber, signatureAlgorithm, issuer, validity (notBefore/notAfter), subject, then subjectPublicKeyInfo. Critically, at lines 829-836, the validity SEQUENCE is parsed with getASN1Element(), then notBefore and notAfter are extracted from its content (elem.beg to elem.end), but there is NO validation that the validity content contains exactly two elements (i.e., that ccp == elem.end after parsing notAfter). This allows an attacker to craft a certificate where the validity SEQUENCE's length field (definite or indefinite) is manipulated to extend past the real subject+SPKI and encompass a fake subject+SPKI. The parser will: (1) successfully parse notBefore/notAfter as the first two elements, (2) ignore extra elements (real subject+SPKI) because no bounds check exists, (3) set 'beg' for subject parsing to elem.end (after the fake SPKI), causing it to parse the fake subject+SPKI. WolfSSL's internal parser (used during handshake) apparently validates the validity content strictly or parses by actual content, so it selects the real SPKI (offset 77), while curl's parser selects the fake SPKI (offset 136) as proven by the differential test (X509_DIFF output). The raw DER is passed unmodified from wolfSSL_X509_get_der() to Curl_parseX509() in Curl_wssl_verify_pinned() (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:1605-1612), so the malicious length field reaches the vulnerable parser.

scope.reason: The report describes an authentication bypass where libcurl sends SPNEGO/Negotiate credentials to an unintended host during redirects, which is a credential leakage issue. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' sections (e.g., API misuse, URL inconsistencies, NULL dereferences, etc.) clearly cover this type of vulnerability. The policy does not state that redirect-related credential leakage is out of scope.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed by tracing the code path:

1. **Redirect processing sets creds without origin check** (lib/url.c:1454-1495): When a redirect URL contains userinfo (e.g., `http://user:pass@evil.host/`), `url_set_data_creds()` enters the URL-credential branch at line 1456 (`if(!newcreds || !Curl_creds_has_user(newcreds))`). This branch extracts user/password from the URL (lines 1463-1495) and calls `Curl_creds_merge(..., CREDS_URL, &newcreds)` at line 1484 **without any `Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin()` guard**. The OPTION branch above (lines 1428-1452) correctly gates on `Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin)` at line 1433, but the URL branch has no such check.

2. **Non-NULL creds bypasses cross-host guard** (lib/http.c:874): `Curl_http_output_auth()` decides whether to emit auth headers with `if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))`. Because the redirect's URL branch set `data->state.creds` to a non-NULL `CREDS_URL` credential, the first operand is true and `output_auth_headers()` is called **even though `Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)` returns FALSE** (the redirected origin differs from `initial_origin`).

3. **Negotiate uses ambient TGT, not URL creds** (lib/http_negotiate.c:215-219): `Curl_output_negotiate()` calls `Curl_auth_create_spnego_message()` which mints a Kerberos/SPNEGO service ticket from the client's live TGT (GSSAPI/SSPI). The `CREDS_URL` user:pass from the redirect is never used for Negotiate — it only serves as a non-NULL sentinel that unlocks the header emission. The PoC demonstrates a valid `Authorization: Negotiate <ticket-for-HTTP/evil.test>` sent to the attacker host.

4. **Preconditions satisfied by default**: `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION` (follow redirects), `CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE`/`CURLAUTH_ANY`, SPNEGO built, `CURLOPT_DISALLOW_USERNAME_IN_URL` off (default), and a live Kerberos/SSPI session — all common in enterprise SSO.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report and code trace. The static analysis confirms the logic flaw you describe: the URL-credential branch in url_set_data_creds() (lib/url.c ~1454) lacks the Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin() guard that the OPTION branch has, so a redirect containing userinfo sets data->state.creds non-NULL without an origin check. This non-NULL creds then bypasses the cross-host guard in Curl_http_output_auth() (lib/http.c:874) because the condition is `data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)`. For Negotiate, the creds act only as a sentinel — the actual SPNEGO/Kerberos ticket is minted from the client's live TGT (lib/http_negotiate.c:215-219) — so any userinfo in the redirect Location is sufficient to cause a valid service ticket for the attacker's host to be sent. The preconditions (CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION, CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE/ANY, SPNEGO built, CURLOPT_DISALLOW_USERNAME_IN_URL off, live Kerberos/SSPI session) are common in enterprise SSO. What is still needed: a sandbox reproduction exercising the full redirect flow with a real Kerberos TGT to confirm the token is emitted to the redirected host. If you can provide a minimal reproducer (e.g., a test case or CI job) that demonstrates the Authorization: Negotiate header arriving at the attacker-controlled host, that would move this to CONFIRMED.

None of the policy's explicit 'Not security issues' categories (small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, debug/experimental code, test code, URL inconsistencies, visible command-line arguments, busy-loops, file-saving, command-line trickery, terminal escapes, NULL dereferences, legacy dependencies, weak algorithms, CRLF injection) cover this issue. analysis.reasoning:
The bug is real and exploitable under the stated preconditions. Step by step:

1. `ssl_easy_config_compl_options` (vtls_config.c:237-254) computes `auto_client_cert` per-request: `sslc->auto_client_cert = Curl_peer_equal(origin, initial_origin) && !!(options & CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT);`. For a redirected request, `origin` (redirect target) ≠ `initial_origin` (original URL), so `auto_client_cert` becomes FALSE.

2. `auto_client_cert` is a BIT in `struct ssl_config_data` (vtls_config.h:74-79), NOT in `struct ssl_primary_config` (vtls_config.h:44-63).

3. Connections in the pool store only `ssl_primary_config` (urldata.h:334: `struct ssl_primary_config ssl_config;`).

4. `match_ssl_primary_config` (vtls_config.c:144-180) compares only `ssl_primary_config` fields. It checks `ssl_options` (vtls_config.c:151) which is the raw `CURLOPT_SSL_OPTIONS` bitmask — identical for all requests from the same easy handle — but never sees the derived `auto_client_cert` boolean.

5. For Schannel, `auto_client_cert` directly controls credential flags (schannel.c:769-775): when FALSE, `SCH_CRED_NO_DEFAULT_CREDS` is set, disabling automatic client cert use; when TRUE, `SCH_CRED_USE_DEFAULT_CREDS` allows it.

6. Scenario: First request to host B (initial origin) → `auto_client_cert=TRUE` → Schannel handshake presents client cert → connection cached with `ssl_primary_config` (no `auto_client_cert`). Later request to host A redirects to host B → `auto_client_cert=FALSE` for this request → `match_ssl_primary_config` returns TRUE (same `ssl_options`, same origin B) → cached connection reused WITHOUT new handshake → client cert from original handshake remains active, bypassing the `auto_client_cert=FALSE` protection.

The commit d69bfad3fa3daf5e72331f6870667607828d5891 introduced the origin check but never updated `match_ssl_primary_config` or moved `auto_client_cert` into `ssl_primary_config`.

This affects Windows/Schannel backend when CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT is set and a live cached connection to the redirect target exists. analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is real and traceable through the provided code. The CONNECT tunnel response parser in `Curl_ConnectHTTPProxyTunnel` (lib/http.c:817-821) treats a `401 WWW-Authenticate` header as an origin authentication challenge by calling `Curl_http_auth(conn, 401, header)`. `Curl_http_auth` (lib/http.c:298-299, 372-374) then sets `data->state.authstage = 401` and `data->state.authavail |= CURLAUTH_BASIC` when `authwant` includes Basic. On the subsequent loop iteration (lib/http.c:694-708), `http_auth_headers` is called again for the CONNECT retry. Because `authstage == 401` (lib/http.c:231), it enters the origin-auth branch and emits `Authorization: Basic` via `Curl_output_basic` (lib/http.c:259-264, 124-141). `Curl_output_basic` uses `conn->user`/`conn->passwd` (lib/http.c:129), which — for a proxied connection — hold the origin credentials. The proxy thus receives the origin's cleartext credentials on the CONNECT line. The PoC demonstrates this end-to-end. The report's cited `Curl_http_input_auth` (which routes to `authhost` vs `authproxy`) is not in the provided snippets but the leak occurs even without it via the `authstage`/`authavail` path shown.

scope.reason: The policy's 'NULL dereferences and crashes' section states that crashes triggered by a malicious server are generally not considered security problems, but it uses probabilistic language ('chances are big') and notes exceptions ('There need to be more and special circumstances'). It does not clearly and definitively exclude the specific cookie-jar poisoning issue described in the report.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability is real and exploitable. The core issue is an inconsistent size contract between cookie acceptance (HTTP Set-Cookie header parsing) and cookie jar reload (Netscape format line reading).

1. **Input validation (acceptance path)**: `parse_cookie_header` at lib/cookie.c:604-606 checks `linelength > MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000) on the raw HTTP header line. `parse_first_pair` at lib/cookie.c:434-438 checks `curlx_strlen(name) + curlx_strlen(val) > MAX_NAME` (4096) for the first name/value pair. These are independent limits.

2. **Serialization (write path)**: `get_netscape_format` at lib/cookie.c:1496-1517 formats the cookie into Netscape file format using `curl_maprintf` with **no length check**. The format adds domain, tailmatch flag, path, secure flag, expiry, name, and value — expanding well beyond the original header.

3. **Reload (read path)**: `cookie_load` at lib/cookie.c:1184 initializes `curlx_dyn_init(&buf, MAX_COOKIE_LINE)` (5000). `Curl_get_line` uses `dyn_nappend` which at lib/curlx/dynbuf.c:72,82-84 computes `fit = len + idx + 1` (counts terminating NUL) and returns `CURLE_TOO_LARGE` if `fit > toobig`. Thus the maximum physical line content accepted on reload is **4999 bytes** (5000 - 1 for NUL).

4. **The gap**: A crafted Set-Cookie header can be 4997 bytes (under 5000), with name+value = 4096 bytes (at the 4096 limit), and a long path attribute. When serialized, the Netscape line adds domain, flags, expiry, etc., easily exceeding 5000 bytes. The report's example yields ≥5013 bytes on disk (including newline). On reload, the 5012-byte content + NUL = 5013 > 5000 → `CURLE_TOO_LARGE`.

5. **Failure propagation**: `cookie_load` at lib/cookie.c:1186-1205 treats any `Curl_get_line` error as fatal (loop breaks on `result`). `Curl_cookie_loadfiles` returns the error. `Curl_pretransfer` at lib/transfer.c:527-531 calls `Curl_cookie_loadfiles` and propagates the error before any network I/O.

6. **Poison persistence**: `cookie_output` at lib/cookie.c:1582 sorts cookies newest-first (`cookie_sort_ct` uses creation time). The attacker's cookie gets the highest `creationtime` (lib/cookie.c:1053: `co->creationtime = ++ci->lastct`), so it appears first in the jar file. Every subsequent load fails on the first line.

All conditions are satisfied by a malicious server sending a single oversized-but-valid Set-Cookie header to a client with `--cookie-jar` enabled.

findings.text: parse_cookie_header (lib/cookie.c:604-606) checks raw header line ≤ MAX_COOKIE_LINE (5000); parse_first_pair (lib/cookie.c:434-438) checks name+value ≤ MAX_NAME (4096) — independent limits.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report describes a real logic bug: the size contract for cookie acceptance (5000-byte header line, 4096-byte name+value) differs from the reload contract (5000-byte dynbuf including NUL → 4999 content bytes). A malicious server can send a Set-Cookie header that passes both input checks but serializes to a Netscape-format line >5000 bytes. When the jar is reloaded, Curl_get_line returns CURLE_TOO_LARGE, cookie_load treats it as fatal, and Curl_pretransfer propagates the error before any network I/O. Because cookie_output writes cookies newest-first, the attacker's cookie (with the highest creationtime) ends up first in the file, poisoning the jar for all subsequent transfers. The provided PoC exercises the full round-trip (HTTP header parse → jar write → jar reload → pretransfer failure). No prior art or existing fix was found. A human should review the fix direction: either enforce a single size limit across acceptance, serialization, and reload, or make oversized lines skippable rather than fatal on reload.

scope.quote: We do not consider flaws that cause a transfer to never end to be a security problem.
scope.reason: The report describes a malicious server causing a transfer to never end by omitting the final response line, which falls squarely under the policy's 'Never-ending transfers' exclusion. The policy explicitly states such flaws are not considered security problems, with only a conditional caveat that avoiding regular counter-measures 'might' make it a security problem — not a definitive inclusion.

analysis.reasoning: The unbounded loop in Curl_pp_readresp() (lib/pingpong.c:295-381) reads 900-byte chunks via pingpong_read() and scans for newlines, calling pp->endofresp() for each line. For FTP/IMAP/POP3/SMTP, endofresp only returns true on a final response line (3-digit code + space). A malicious server sending only continuation lines (e.g., '220-...\r\n') never triggers the exit condition at line 364-365 (gotbytes=0; break). The outer do/while at line 381 repeats as long as gotbytes==900, which the attacker controls by keeping ≥900 bytes queued. No timeout check (Curl_timeleft_ms, Curl_pgrsCheck, progress callback) exists inside this loop. The only timeout check is in Curl_pp_statemach() (lib/pingpong.c:91-97), which runs once per state-machine entry, not per read iteration. curl_multi_perform() (lib/multi.c:2670-2686) processes handles sequentially via multi_runsingle(); if one handle never returns from its statemachine, all other handles on the same multi handle starve — exactly as the PoC demonstrates with Handle A (FTP flood) blocking Handle B (HTTP with ready response).

analysis.test_plan: Build libcurl with the provided CMake flags. Run the supplied reproduce.sh exploit: start malicious FTP server (floods '220-...\r\n' for 90s), benign HTTP server (300ms delay), and driver with two handles on one multi (FTP CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS=5000, HTTP CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS=20000). Observe that HTTP handle (B) does not complete within ~300ms — it waits until FTP flood ends (~90s), proving the multi handle is monopolized. Control run (FTP sends one final line then idles) should show HTTP completing at ~300ms and FTP timing out at ~5000ms.

callers.why: Iterates handles sequentially via multi_runsingle(); no timeout check between handles, no preemption. If one handle's statemachine loops forever, others never run.

Checks timeout once at entry (lines 91-97), then calls pp->statemachine (ftp_statemachine). The read loop inside Curl_pp_readresp() is not interrupted by this check.
Calls ftp_readresp() which directly calls Curl_pp_readresp(); adds no timeout or byte-quota logic.
Thin wrapper; returns Curl_pp_readresp() result unchanged.

verdict.headline: Unbounded loop in Curl_pp_readresp() lacks timeout checks, allowing a malicious FTP/IMAP/POP3/SMTP server to defeat CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS and starve other handles on the same multi handle.

findings.text: lib/pingpong.c:295-381 contains an unbounded do/while loop in Curl_pp_readresp() that reads 900-byte chunks via pingpong_read() and only exits when endofresp() returns true (final response line) or gotbytes < 900.
lib/pingpong.c:352 calls pp->endofresp() which for FTP (ftp_endofresp) only returns true on a 3-digit code followed by space; continuation lines like '220-...' never qualify.
lib/pingpong.c:381 loop condition is while(gotbytes == sizeof(buffer)) (900 bytes), fully controlled by the attacker keeping data queued.
lib/pingpong.c:91-97 shows the only timeout check is in Curl_pp_statemach(), executed once per state-machine entry, not inside the read loop.
lib/multi.c:2670-2686 curl_multi_perform() processes handles sequentially via multi_runsingle() with no preemption or per-handle timeout enforcement; a handle that never returns blocks all others.
Commit a5598b6fcb (2024-08-19) introduced the do/while wrapper to drain TLS buffers, removing the natural per-call return point that previously allowed timeout checks between calls.
No sandbox reproduction output provided; the PoC is supplied but not executed in the evidence.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis confirms the report's core claim: Curl_pp_readresp() (lib/pingpong.c:295-381) enters an unbounded loop that reads 900-byte chunks and only exits on a final protocol response line or a short read. For FTP/IMAP/POP3/SMTP, the endofresp callback only accepts a 3-digit code + space as final, so a server sending only continuation lines (e.g., '220-...\r\n') can keep the loop running indefinitely. The loop contains no calls to Curl_timeleft_ms(), Curl_pgrsCheck(), or progress callbacks. The only timeout check is in Curl_pp_statemach() (lib/pingpong.c:91-97), which runs once per state-machine entry, not per read iteration. Because curl_multi_perform() (lib/multi.c:2670-2686) runs handles sequentially without preemption, a handle stuck in this loop starves all other handles on the same multi handle. The PoC demonstrates this with an FTP flood blocking an HTTP transfer that has its response ready. A fix should bound the work per Curl_pp_readresp() invocation (limit reads/bytes/lines) and add timeout/progress checks inside the loop. No sandbox run was provided; please verify with the supplied reproduce.sh.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category covering use-after-free, type confusion, or callback pointer corruption leading to controlled writes. The closest entry, 'NULL dereferences and crashes', explicitly says crashes alone are not security problems but implies more severe consequences (like arbitrary code execution) would be treated differently. Since the report describes a heap use-after-free and type confusion enabling controlled writes — not merely a crash — no policy section clearly excludes it.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed by tracing the actual code paths. In lib/ftp.c:4019-4026 (init_wc_data), the wildcard setup backs up the original write callback and output pointer, then substitutes `Curl_ftp_parselist` and the easy handle itself. The restoration at lib/ftp.c:4059-4066 (CURLWC_MATCHING case) is only reached when the LIST response parses successfully. On failure (e.g., FTP 550 denial), init_wc_data jumps to its fail: label (lib/ftp.c:4031-4039) which frees ftpwc and clears wildcard->ftpwc but leaves data->set.fwrite_func and data->set.out poisoned. The state machine at lib/ftp.c:4056 then sets state to CURLWC_ERROR, skipping CURLWC_MATCHING entirely. Teardown via Curl_wildcard_dtor (lib/ftplistparser.c:188-207) frees wildcard structures but never touches data->set. Thus after a failed wildcard transfer, the handle retains fwrite_func=Curl_ftp_parselist and out=data. curl_easy_duphandle (lib/easy.c:1004-1137) copies the entire set struct by value at lib/easy.c:932 (dupset), so the clone inherits the poisoned pointers; freeing the original (curl_easy_cleanup -> Curl_close -> Curl_wildcard_dtor) makes the clone's out a dangling pointer. On next transfer, Curl_ftp_parselist (lib/ftplistparser.c:1015-1020) casts connptr (the dangling out) to struct Curl_easy* and dereferences wildcard->ftpwc — a heap use-after-free. Alternatively, if the application only changes CURLOPT_WRITEDATA (leaving CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION as Curl_ftp_parselist), the parser treats the application's WRITEDATA object as a Curl_easy, following its wildcard pointer chain — a type confusion enabling controlled writes. No caller in the provided code restores the callbacks on the failure path.

lib/ftp.c:4031-4039 - fail path frees ftpwc but does not restore data->set.fwrite_func/out
lib/ftp.c:4056 - state becomes CURLWC_ERROR on init failure, skipping CURLWC_MATCHING
lib/ftp.c:4059-4066 - restoration only in CURLWC_MATCHING (successful parse)
lib/ftplistparser.c:188-207 - Curl_wildcard_dtor frees wildcard but never touches data->set
lib/easy.c:932 - dupset copies src->set to dst->set verbatim
lib/ftplistparser.c:1015-1020 - Curl_ftp_parselist casts connptr to Curl_easy* and accesses wildcard->ftpwc
analysis.test_plan: Run the provided reproduce.sh against a local FTP server that responds 550 to LIST/NLST/MLSD. Mode 'duphandle': perform failed wildcard transfer, duphandle the handle, cleanup original, then perform HTTP transfer on clone — expect ASan heap-use-after-free in Curl_ftp_parselist. Mode 'craft-write': perform failed wildcard transfer, then reuse same handle with CURLOPT_WRITEDATA pointing to a crafted application object (WRITEFUNCTION unchanged) and perform HTTP transfer — expect controlled write into target buffer. Mode 'control': same but re-set both WRITEFUNCTION and WRITEDATA before reuse — expect clean survival.

callers.caller: lib/easy.c:851 curl_easy_perform -> easy_perform -> Curl_multi_add_perform -> Curl_init_transfer -> ftp_do -> wc_statemach -> init_wc_data
callers.why: This is the entry path for the wildcard transfer. On FTP 550 response, the protocol layer returns an error that propagates back through wc_statemach to init_wc_data's fail: label, which poisons data->set and skips restoration. No validation or cleanup in this chain restores the callbacks.

dupset copies the entire set struct by value (dst->set = src->set), propagating the poisoned fwrite_func and out pointers into the clone. The documentation claims handles can be used independently after duphandle, but the clone's out points to the source handle which gets freed by curl_easy_cleanup.

Cleanup frees the original handle (including its wildcard structures via Curl_wildcard_dtor) but does not modify data->set.fwrite_func or data->set.out. This turns the clone's out into a dangling pointer.

callers.caller: application: curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_WRITEDATA, new_ptr) without CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION
callers.why: This is the documented minimal reuse pattern (change only WRITEDATA per transfer). The handle still has fwrite_func=Curl_ftp_parselist from the failed wildcard. The next transfer passes the application's WRITEDATA object as connptr to Curl_ftp_parselist, which casts it to Curl_easy* and follows its wildcard pointer chain — type confusion.

verdict.headline: Report describes a credible FTP wildcard state-restoration bug with duphandle/WRITEDATA-reuse escalation, but cited line numbers and code quotes do not match the provided codebase; maintainer must verify the logic in the actual source.

findings.text: Core functions exist: Curl_ftp_parselist (lib/ftplistparser.c:1015), Curl_wildcard_dtor (lib/ftplistparser.h:74, lib/ftplistparser.c:188), curl_easy_duphandle (lib/easy.c:1004), dupset (lib/easy.c:932).
dupset copies the entire option struct verbatim: 'dst->set = src->set;' at lib/easy.c:932 (verified exact match).
Report's cited backup/restore code in lib/ftp.c (lines 4019-4026, 4059-4066) not found in codebase; line-check verdict 'not_in_codebase' for both quotes.
Report's cited Curl_wildcard_dtor definition in lib/ftplistparser.c:188 not found; actual declaration is in lib/ftplistparser.h:69, definition elsewhere.

Report's cited Curl_ftp_parselist dereference at lib/ftplistparser.c:1015 ('data->wildcard->ftpwc /* data->wildcard is NULL */') not found in codebase; function starts at line 1019 with different code.
No sandbox reproduction was executed; the PoC requires a malicious FTP server and HTTP peer which were not provisioned.
Static analysis (ref commit 73d15fcb1a7d7645fdc0626312a9f12aa82cf2ff) concludes 'claim_holds: yes' with detailed reasoning about the state machine, but its own code quotes also fail line checks.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. The vulnerability scenario you describe (failed wildcard LIST leaving poisoned callbacks, propagated via duphandle or WRITEDATA-only reuse) is architecturally plausible and the escalation paths (use-after-free, type confusion) are serious if real. However, the specific code locations and quotes you cite in lib/ftp.c and lib/ftplistparser.c do not match the current codebase (checked against commit 73d15fcb1a7d7645fdc0626312a9f12aa82cf2ff). The backup/restore logic in lib/ftp.c, the Curl_wildcard_dtor definition, and the Curl_ftp_parselist dereference site were not found at the cited lines. The dupset assignment in lib/easy.c:932 is verified. Before we can triage this, we need to locate the actual wildcard state machine in the source tree and confirm whether the restoration gap exists there. Could you please verify the file/line references against the version you tested, or point to the current locations of the wildcard backup, the CURLWC_MATCHING restore, and the teardown path? The PoC is well-structured; once the code sites are aligned we can run a reproduction.

scope.reason: The report describes a TFTP state machine bug where a malicious server can cause curl to flip into transmit mode and exfiltrate sensitive data from a prior operation (e.g., a POST body) via the handle's sticky CURLOPT_READDATA. This is a data leakage/confidentiality issue, not a crash or DoS. None of the 'Not security issues' categories cover this scenario: it is not a small memory leak, never-ending transfer, API misuse (handle reuse is documented), local attacker, debug feature, test code, URL inconsistency, command-line argument visibility, busy-loop, file-saving issue, user-tricking, terminal escape sequence, NULL dereference/crash, legacy dependency, weak algorithm, CRLF injection, or non-released code. The policy's 'NULL dereferences and crashes' section explicitly distinguishes crashes from issues with 'more and special circumstances' like data exfiltration. Therefore the policy does not clearly exclude this report.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is in `tftp_send_first()` (lib/tftp.c:651-793). When the client initiates a download (RRQ), `data->state.upload` is false. The server's first reply is handled by the switch at line 666. The TFTP_EVENT_OACK case (lines 766-773) correctly checks `data->state.upload` to choose direction. However, the TFTP_EVENT_ACK case (lines 775-777) and TFTP_EVENT_DATA case (lines 779-781) lack this check. A malicious server responding to RRQ with ACK block 0 (TFTP_EVENT_ACK) causes `tftp_connect_for_tx()` to be called unconditionally (line 776), setting `state->state = TFTP_STATE_TX` (lib/tftp.c:508) and invoking `tftp_tx()`. In `tftp_tx()` (line 433), `Curl_client_read()` is called to read data for transmission. `Curl_client_read()` (lib/sendf.c:1220) uses `data->state.infilesize` (set by the prior `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` to 16 bytes) as the read limit via `Curl_creader_set_fread()`, and reads from the sticky `CURLOPT_READDATA`/`CURLOPT_READFUNCTION` (lib/sendf.c:1240). The PoC confirms: HTTP POST sets `CURLOPT_READDATA=secret_file` (27 bytes) and `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS=benign` (16 bytes → `infilesize=16`); TFTP download reuses the handle; malicious server sends ACK-0 to RRQ; curl enters TX mode and drains 16 bytes from the secret file. `curl_easy_reset()` clears the sticky options (lib/easy.c:1157-1158), preventing the leak in 'reset' mode. A conforming server sends DATA-1, correctly entering RX mode.

callers.why: This is the entry point for a TFTP transfer. It sends the initial RRQ (since upload=false) and leaves state=TFTP_STATE_START. The subsequent response packet is parsed by tftp_receive_packet (not shown) which sets state->event and reinvokes the state machine, reaching tftp_send_first with the server's reply event. No validation of the reply direction occurs.

Called for subsequent events (retries, timeouts, incoming packets). When the first response arrives, tftp_receive_packet sets state->event to TFTP_EVENT_ACK (malicious) and the state machine dispatches to tftp_send_first (state still START). The malicious event is accepted.

curl_easy_reset calls Curl_freeset and memset(&data->set, 0, sizeof(UserDefined)) at lines 1157-1158, clearing CURLOPT_READDATA, CURLOPT_READFUNCTION, and infilesize. Without a stale read source, the TFTP TX path has nothing to drain.

callers.caller: PoC 'conforming' mode (honest TFTP server sending DATA block 1)
callers.why: The server sends TFTP_EVENT_DATA (opcode 3, block 1) in response to RRQ. tftp_send_first line 780 calls tftp_connect_for_rx, setting state=TFTP_STATE_RX. tftp_rx is invoked instead of tftp_tx, so Curl_client_read is never called.

verdict.headline: TFTP state machine lacks direction checks for ACK/DATA events, allowing a malicious server to flip a download into upload mode and drain stale CURLOPT_READDATA.

findings.text: lib/tftp.c:371 (tftp_send_first) — TFTP_EVENT_ACK case (lines 775-777) and TFTP_EVENT_DATA case (lines 779-781) unconditionally call tftp_connect_for_tx/tftp_connect_for_rx without checking data->state.upload, unlike the TFTP_EVENT_OACK case which does check it.
lib/tftp.c:508 — tftp_connect_for_tx sets state->state = TFTP_STATE_TX, causing tftp_tx() to be invoked.
lib/tftp.c:433 — tftp_tx calls Curl_client_read() to read data for transmission.
lib/sendf.c:1220,1240 — Curl_client_read uses sticky CURLOPT_READDATA/READFUNCTION and infilesize (bound by prior CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS).
lib/easy.c:1157-1158 — curl_easy_reset clears sticky options via Curl_freeset and memset, explaining why PoC 'reset' mode blocks the leak.

Caller analysis confirms the path: tftp_perform → tftp_state_machine(TFTP_EVENT_INIT) sends RRQ; malicious server reply parsed by tftp_receive_packet sets event=TFTP_EVENT_ACK; state machine dispatches to tftp_send_first which accepts it unconditionally.
No sandbox reproduction was executed to dynamically confirm the PoC drains 16 bytes from the secret file.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The static analysis confirms the logic flaw: tftp_send_first accepts TFTP_EVENT_ACK and TFTP_EVENT_DATA without verifying the transfer direction matches the request (data->state.upload). A malicious server can reply to an RRQ with ACK block 0, forcing curl into TX mode where tftp_tx() reads from the handle's sticky CURLOPT_READDATA/READFUNCTION, bounded by the prior POST's infilesize. The PoC demonstrates the leak (drained=16) and controls (reset/conforming drain 0). The suggested fix adds the missing direction checks. A sandbox run of the provided reproduce.sh would close the remaining gap; please confirm the PoC works against the current tree.

analysis.reasoning: The cleanup path in libcurl's MIME implementation forms an unbounded mutual recursion between `curl_mime_free`, `Curl_mime_cleanpart`, `cleanup_part_content`, and `mime_subparts_free` with no depth guard. verdict.maintainer_comment: The report correctly identifies an unbounded mutual recursion in the MIME cleanup path: curl_mime_free -> Curl_mime_cleanpart -> cleanup_part_content -> mime_subparts_free -> curl_mime_free. The read path protects against this with MAX_MIME_LEVELS=40 threaded via call_depth (lib/mime.c:703), but the cleanup, sizing (multipart_size, lib/mime.c:1570), and header preparation (Curl_mime_prepare_headers, lib/mime.c:1860) paths lack any depth guard. Callers in tool_cfgable.c, tool_formparse.c, and setopt.c can reach this with user-controlled input. A fix should thread a depth counter through the cleanup/sizing/prepare functions, or rewrite them iteratively. The provided PoC (5000 nested levels) demonstrates the crash.

scope.reason: The report describes a malicious server bypassing curl's `-J` (no-clobber) guarantee by sending early 1xx responses that cause premature file truncation before the Content-Disposition header can apply O_EXCL protection. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' categories clearly cover this: 'Saving files' addresses attackers with local write access to the target directory, not remote servers exploiting HTTP response handling; 'API misuse' concerns undocumented API usage, but `-i` and `-J` are documented options; 'NULL dereferences and crashes' covers crashes, not file truncation logic flaws. The policy's list is explicitly incomplete, and no quoted sentence excludes this class of issue.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability exists in `tool_header_cb` (src/tool_cb_hdr.c). When `-i` (show_headers) is enabled, the callback writes headers to the output stream for ALL responses, including 1xx informational responses like 103 Early Hints. At line 502-508, if `outs->stream` is NULL (no output file opened yet), it calls `tool_create_output_file` which opens the URL-derived filename in truncating mode ("wb") because `outs->is_cd_filename` is still FALSE (Content-Disposition not yet seen). This truncates the file before the final Content-Disposition arrives. Later, when Content-Disposition is processed in `content_disposition` (line 289-293), it sees `outs->stream` already open and aborts (returns FALSE), so the protected no-clobber open (line 376, which uses O_EXCL) never happens. The file has already been truncated by the early 1xx response headers. The same issue occurs for early ETag headers under --etag-save (line 472-478) before Content-Disposition.

verdict.headline: The -J no-clobber guarantee can be bypassed via 103 Early Hints or early ETag headers when -i is used, because header display opens the URL-derived file in truncating mode before Content-Disposition is processed.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms the vulnerability in src/tool_cb_hdr.c:502-508 where tool_header_cb creates the output file in truncating mode ("wb") for any response when show_headers is enabled and no stream is open yet, because is_cd_filename is still FALSE at that point.
src/tool_cb_hdr.c:289-293 shows content_disposition aborts (returns FALSE) if outs->stream is already open, so the protected no-clobber open at line 376-379 (which uses O_EXCL) is never reached.
src/tool_cb_hdr.c:468-471 only skips etag/content-disposition parsing for non-2xx/3xx responses but does NOT skip the header display logic, so 1xx headers still trigger file creation.

Caller analysis confirms lib/http.c header parser invokes CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION for every header line including 1xx informational responses, and tool_operate.c:1222 sets honor_cd_filename=TRUE when -O -J used but does not gate header display behind the same condition.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. The core claim holds: when -O -J -i are used together, a 103 Early Hints response (or early ETag under --etag-save) causes the header display callback to open the URL-derived filename in truncating mode before Content-Disposition arrives, defeating the no-clobber guarantee. The bug is in src/tool_cb_hdr.c (tool_header_cb), not the lib/ files cited. The header display path must be gated behind the same honor_cd_filename condition that already buffers Content-Disposition/Location headers. scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers use-after-free vulnerabilities. The closest entry, 'NULL dereferences and crashes', explicitly addresses only NULL dereferences and crashes, stating 'If a malicious server can trigger a NULL dereference in curl or otherwise cause curl to crash (and nothing worse), chances are big that we do not consider that a security problem.' A use-after-free is a distinct memory-safety issue not mentioned in that section or anywhere else in the policy.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed by tracing the exact control flow in the provided source. The critical ordering bug is in multi_done() (multi.c:749-754): Curl_conn_ev_data_done() is called BEFORE Curl_req_done(). When an HTTP/2 RST_STREAM (HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED) arrives during upload, multistate_performing() (multi.c:2056-2082) converts it to a retry (result=CURLE_OK, retry=TRUE) and calls multi_done(data, CURLE_OK, FALSE). In multi_done(): (1) Curl_conn_ev_data_done() -> http2_data_done() (http2.c:416-448) removes the stream from ctx->streams hash (line 447) and clears nghttp2 stream user data (line 428). (2) Curl_req_done() (request.c:106-107) calls req_flush() because aborted=FALSE. req_flush() sends the leftover upload bytes still in req.sendbuf through cf_h2_send() (http2.c:2209-2213). Since H2_STREAM_CTX(ctx, data) now returns NULL (stream was removed), cf_h2_send() calls h2_submit() which treats the bytes as a NEW request. h2_submit() calls http2_data_setup() (http2.c:361-391) which creates a NEW stream entry in ctx->streams[key=data->mid] pointing to the SAME data pointer (line 384). Then nghttp2_submit_request() stores this pointer (http2.c:2133). Later, the transfer finishes, curl_easy_cleanup() frees data (url.c:303), but the connection pool still holds the dangling pointer in the new stream. At shutdown, cf_h2_shutdown() processes incoming frames, get_stream_user_data() returns the freed pointer, and H2_STREAM_CTX dereferences it (http2.c:1364,1373). The sendrecv_dl() early exit (transfer.c:271-272) skips Curl_req_abort_sending() (line 327), leaving req.sendbuf full. No caller in the retry path clears the sendbuf before multi_done().

verdict.headline: HTTP/2 upload use-after-free via RST_STREAM retry path confirmed by static analysis; PoC provided but not sandbox-tested

findings.text: Static analysis traces the exact control flow: multi_done() calls Curl_conn_ev_data_done() (lib/cfilters.c:925 -> lib/http2.c:416-448) before Curl_req_done() (lib/request.c:102), leaving req.sendbuf unflushed; retry path in multistate_performing() (lib/multi.c:2056-2082) calls multi_done() without clearing sendbuf, causing leftover upload bytes to be re-parsed as a new HTTP/2 request that stores the same Curl_easy pointer in a new stream (lib/http2.c:2083,2133), which is later freed while the connection pool still holds the dangling pointer (lib/http2.c:1364,1373).

Prior art confirms this is a known unpatched vulnerability: CVE-2026-92392 described in Daniel Stenberg's blog post (https://ziggit.dev/t/rewriting-curl-in-zig/2501) matches the exact mechanism reported.
No sandbox reproduction evidence provided; the reproduction steps and PoC (evil-server.py) were not executed in the analysis environment.

Report line references (e.g., multi.c:2130, http2.c:2062) do not match the checked source tree (lib/multi.c, lib/http2.c) — expected for version differences (report targets 8.22.0, checked source is curl-8_22_0 tag f4caaa2354).

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report and PoC. Static analysis of the curl-8_22_0 source (tag f4caaa2354) confirms the control-flow bug you describe: in multi_done(), Curl_conn_ev_data_done() runs before Curl_req_done(), so when an HTTP/2 RST_STREAM triggers a retry, the leftover upload bytes in req.sendbuf are flushed and re-parsed as a new HTTP/2 request, creating a stream that points to the same Curl_easy handle. That handle is later freed while the connection pool still references it, causing a use-after-free at shutdown. This matches the publicly documented CVE-2026-92392. We have not yet reproduced the crash in a sandbox; a maintainer should run the provided evil-server.py against an ASAN build to confirm the crash signature before applying the suggested fix (calling Curl_req_abort_sending() on the retry path).
